stem: A periodontal probe reads 5 mm from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket. What is this measurement called?
ex: PD runs from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket. CAL adds recession to PD; GR runs from the CEJ to the gingival margin.
why: Probing depth is measured from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket, exactly what this reading describes.
CAL is measured from the CEJ, not the gingival margin: it is probing depth plus recession.
Recession runs from the CEJ to the gingival margin; it says nothing about how deep the pocket is.
Radiographic bone loss is read on a film, not measured with a probe in the pocket.

cue: CAL = PD + GR, and a hidden CEJ makes GR negative: 7 + (-4) = 3.
stem: Probing depth is 7 mm, and the CEJ is felt 4 mm apical to the gingival margin (no visible recession). What is the clinical attachment level?
ex: CAL = PD + GR using signed GR. Here GR = -4 (CEJ is subgingival), so CAL = 7 + (-4) = 3 mm of attachment loss.
why: With the CEJ 4 mm below the margin, GR is -4, so CAL = 7 + (-4) = 3 mm.
7 mm is the probing depth; it ignores the 4 mm of pocket that sits above the CEJ on enamel.
11 mm adds the 4 mm instead of subtracting it; a subgingival CEJ makes GR negative.
4 mm is the CEJ-to-margin distance (the negative recession), not the attachment loss.

likely.t: Stage from CAL and bone loss, never from probing depth alone

stem: Tooth X: 2 mm probing depth with 4 mm of visible recession (CAL 6 mm). Tooth Y: 7 mm probing depth, CEJ felt 4 mm subgingival (CAL 3 mm). Which tooth is more maintainable for the patient?
choices: Tooth X, with 6 mm of CAL
Tooth Y, with 3 mm of CAL
ex: Recession makes CAL look worse on paper, but a shallow, accessible 2 mm pocket is far easier for a patient to brush and floss than a deep 7 mm pocket.
why: A shallow 2 mm pocket is easy for the patient to brush and floss, so it is more maintainable even with more CAL on paper.
A 7 mm pocket is too deep for home care to reach, so it is harder to maintain despite its lower CAL.
The two differ: maintainability depends on pocket depth the patient can clean, not on CAL alone.
Both can be maintained; the question is which is easier, and the shallow pocket wins.

likely.t: Stage from CAL and bone loss, never from probing depth alone

stem: Which radiograph is preferred over a horizontal bitewing when screening for periodontal bone loss, and why?
choices: Vertical bitewing — less likely to miss an arch
Panoramic — gives the most site-specific detail
Occlusal film — best shows interproximal bone
ex: A horizontal bitewing can fail to capture bone loss on one of the two arches; vertical bitewings extend the field and are preferred when bone loss is a concern.
why: Vertical bitewings extend the field, so bone loss on either arch is less likely to be cut off the film.
A panoramic gives an overview but the least site-specific detail of these films.
Occlusal films show the arch from above and are not used to read interproximal crestal bone.
The horizontal bitewing is the one being replaced here: it can miss bone loss on one of the two arches.

stem: Match each recession type to its definition.
ex: Recession types compare interproximal attachment loss with buccal loss. No interproximal loss is RT1 (full root coverage is predictable); interproximal loss no greater than the buccal is RT2 (partial coverage expected); interproximal loss greater than the buccal is RT3 (root coverage is not attempted). Jepsen, Caton et al., 2018 World Workshop, Workgroup 3.

likely.t: Recession types from the chart: RT1, RT2, RT3 and root coverage

stem: Under the 2018 World Workshop classification, what replaced the older separate categories of 'chronic periodontitis' and 'aggressive periodontitis'?
choices: A single "Periodontitis" category, staged and graded
Nothing — the old terms are still used clinically
ex: Both old terms were merged into one Periodontitis category; individualized severity/behavior is now captured through staging and grading instead.
why: Chronic and aggressive periodontitis were merged into one Periodontitis category, described by stage and grade.
There are no 'slow' and 'fast' categories; speed of progression is captured by the grade.
The old terms were retired in the 2017/2018 classification; staging and grading replaced them.
Necrotizing periodontitis is its own separate category, not a merger of chronic and aggressive.

stem: What bleeding-on-probing threshold is used before a case is called gingivitis, to account for inter-examiner probing variability?
ex: Two or three bleeding spots on a full-mouth chart are not, by themselves, enough to diagnose gingivitis.
why: Gingivitis needs bleeding at 10% or more of sites, so a few stray bleeding spots don't make the diagnosis.
Any bleeding at all would over-diagnose; two or three spots can come from probing variability.
50% is far above the cutoff; gingivitis is diagnosed from 10% of sites.
25% is not the threshold; the gingivitis cutoff is 10% of sites bleeding.

stem: A treated periodontitis patient is stable on 3-month maintenance with no bleeding and shallow probing depths, though radiographs show old bone loss. What is the correct diagnosis today?
ex: A stable, well-maintained patient is not re-staged — they are described as healthy on a reduced periodontium.
why: A stable, well-maintained treated patient with no bleeding and shallow pockets has health on a reduced periodontium.
Without bleeding and with shallow pockets the disease is not active; old bone loss alone does not make it active Stage 3.
The periodontium is not intact: there is old bone loss, so it is a reduced periodontium.
Necrotizing disease is painful with necrotic papillae, nothing like this stable patient.

likely.t: Maintenance works: the Becker tooth-loss figures

stem: Which statement about reversibility is correct?
choices: Gingivitis is fully reversible; periodontitis is not
Both gingivitis and periodontitis are fully reversible
Neither gingivitis nor periodontitis is reversible
Periodontitis is fully reversible; gingivitis is not
ex: There is a point of no return between the two: gingivitis resolves completely with plaque control, while periodontitis leaves permanent attachment loss even after successful treatment, so the best result is health on a reduced periodontium, not the original attachment level.
why: Gingivitis resolves fully with plaque control; periodontitis leaves permanent attachment loss, so the best outcome is health on a reduced periodontium.
Periodontitis is not fully reversible: treatment stabilizes it, but lost attachment does not return to its original level.
Gingivitis is reversible: it sits entirely within the gingiva and resolves with plaque control.
This flips them: gingivitis is the reversible one, periodontitis is not.

stem: What grade should a clinician assume by default, before looking for evidence to shift it up or down?
ex: Clinicians should initially assume Grade B (moderate progression) and seek specific evidence to move to A or C.
why: Grade B (moderate progression) is the default; you then look for evidence to move to A or C.
Grade A needs evidence of slow progression; it is not the starting assumption.
Grade C needs evidence of rapid progression or risk factors; it is not the default.
There is a default: assume Grade B until evidence shifts it.

likely.t: Grading: start at B; the bone-loss/age ratio, smoking and HbA1c

stem: A 30-year-old patient has 50% bone loss on their worst tooth. What does that bone-loss/age ratio suggest on its own?
choices: About 1.7, which still falls in Grade B
None: without serial records it can't be graded
ex: % bone loss at the worst tooth ÷ age: 50 ÷ 30 ≈ 1.7. Under 0.25 suggests Grade A, 0.25-1.0 Grade B and over 1.0 Grade C, so this points to rapid progression, Grade C. The ratio is the indirect evidence used when there are no serial records to show progression directly.
why: 50% bone loss ÷ 30 years ≈ 1.7, above the 1.0 cutoff, which points to Grade C.
0.6 comes from dividing age by bone loss (30 ÷ 50); the ratio is % bone loss ÷ age, about 1.7.
Grade B covers 0.25 to 1.0; a ratio of about 1.7 is above 1.0, which is Grade C.
Serial records are the gold standard when they exist; without them, the bone-loss/age ratio is exactly what you use.

likely.t: Grading: start at B; the bone-loss/age ratio, smoking and HbA1c

cue: Bone loss outpacing age (ratio over 1) = Grade C on its own, no smoking or diabetes needed.
stem: Case A (30-year-old, systemically healthy) has isolated bone loss into the middle third of the root at #30 with a 7 mm probing depth, and no smoking or diabetes. What is her diagnosis?
ex: Middle-third bone loss and a 7 mm pocket put her in Stage 3, and one involved tooth makes it localized. Grade: middle-third loss is more than 33% of the root, so at age 30 the bone-loss/age ratio is over 1, which is Grade C even without smoking or diabetes. The tempting wrong answer is Grade B: a healthy nonsmoker still gets Grade C when bone loss outpaces age.
why: Middle-third bone loss with a 7 mm pocket is Stage 3, one tooth makes it localized, and losing more than a third of the root by age 30 is a ratio over 1, which is Grade C.
No modifier is needed for Grade C: more than a third of the root lost at age 30 gives a bone-loss/age ratio over 1, which is Grade C by itself.
Her bone loss is isolated to #30, far under 30% of her teeth, so it is localized, not generalized.
Stage 2 stops at bone loss in the coronal third; bone loss into the middle third with a 7 mm pocket is Stage 3.

likely.t: Grading: start at B; the bone-loss/age ratio, smoking and HbA1c

stem: Case E has an HbA1c of 6.1%. Why does her periodontitis stay Grade B instead of moving to Grade C?
choices: Her HbA1c is below the 7% cutoff for Grade C
Diabetes is never a grade modifier
Only heavy smoking can push a case to Grade C
Diabetes moves the stage, not the grade
ex: The diabetes grade modifier only applies at an HbA1c of 7% or more. At 6.1% her control is good enough that diabetes isn't acting as a modifier, so her grade rests on the bone-loss/age ratio and stays B. Diabetes is still a grade factor, never a stage factor; it just isn't triggered below 7%.
why: The diabetes modifier applies only at an HbA1c of 7% or more; at 6.1% it doesn't push her to Grade C.
Diabetes is a grade modifier: an HbA1c of 7% or more pushes a case to Grade C.
Heavy smoking is one route to Grade C; an HbA1c of 7% or more and a bone-loss/age ratio over 1.0 are others.
Diabetes is a grade modifier; the stage comes from CAL, bone loss, teeth lost and complexity.

likely.t: Grading: start at B; the bone-loss/age ratio, smoking and HbA1c

cue: "Screen, Stage, Grade, Plan": a quick look, then fine-tune the stage, then the grade, then treat.
stem: Put the 4-step approach to diagnosing periodontitis in order.
steps: Initial screening of full-mouth radiographs, probing depths, and missing teeth
Fine-tune the stage using maximum CAL/RBL and case complexity
Determine the grade from progression evidence and modifiers
Build the treatment plan from the stage and grade
ex: The four-step workflow in the Review table: first screen the full-mouth radiographs, probing depths and missing teeth to sort the case into Stage 1-2 or Stage 3-4; then fine-tune the stage from the maximum CAL/RBL, horizontal vs vertical bone loss, teeth lost and complexity; then set the grade (assume B and shift with evidence and modifiers); then plan treatment: Stage 1-2 gets standard periodontal treatment, Stage 3-4 complex or multidisciplinary care.

stem: At flap reflection, bone remains on the buccal wall, the lingual wall, and against the neighboring tooth — only the involved root surface itself lacks bone. How many walls does this defect have, and what does that mean for regeneration?
choices: 3 walls — the best prognosis for regeneration
1 wall — the worst prognosis for regeneration
2 walls — the interdental pattern called a crater
4 walls — bone on all sides of the defect
ex: The more walls remaining around a defect, the better the case for regrowing bone, PDL, and cementum.
why: Buccal, lingual and proximal walls remain: a 3-wall defect, which has the best prognosis for regeneration.
A 1-wall defect has only one wall left and the worst prognosis; this one has three.
A crater is a 2-wall defect with bone lost on both proximal surfaces; here the wall against the neighboring tooth still stands.
There is no fourth bony wall here: the fourth side of this defect is the bare root surface, so it is a 3-wall defect.

cue: Crater = a dip between two teeth: both proximal walls gone, buccal and lingual left standing.
stem: Bone is lost on both proximal root surfaces of a defect, leaving only the buccal and lingual walls. What is this specific 2-wall pattern called?
ex: When both neighboring teeth have lost bone at the same site, the resulting 2-wall defect is called a crater.
why: A 2-wall defect with bone lost on both proximal sides, leaving buccal and lingual walls, is a crater.
A hemiseptum is a 1-wall defect between two teeth; a crater keeps two walls, the buccal and the lingual.
A furcation is bone loss between the roots of a multirooted tooth, not between neighboring teeth.
A dehiscence is missing bone over the facial or lingual root surface, not an interdental crater.

cue: "Temp, Treat, Then crown": no permanent crown until perio therapy is finished.
stem: A patient needs both a crown and periodontal therapy on the same tooth. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Temporary crown → complete periodontal therapy → definitive crown
Definitive crown first, then periodontal therapy
Skip the crown until therapy is finished, no temporary needed
Temporary and definitive crowns can both be placed alongside SRP
ex: Never place a permanent crown before periodontal therapy is complete — a temporary bridges the gap, and the same logic applies to a final RPD.
why: Place a temporary, finish periodontal therapy, then deliver the definitive crown once the tissue is stable.
A permanent crown is never placed before periodontal therapy is complete; the margins depend on healed tissue.
The tooth still needs protection and function; a temporary crown bridges the gap during therapy.
Only the temporary goes in alongside therapy; the definitive crown waits until therapy is finished.

likely.t: Caries control is part of Phase I; the treatment sequence

stem: Where does caries control fit in the treatment sequence?
choices: It is part of Phase I therapy, alongside SRP
It only happens after all surgical therapy is finished
It is unrelated to periodontal treatment planning
It always follows delivery of the final RPD
ex: A cavitated surface is harder to instrument and harder for the patient to keep clean, so restoring it is bundled into Phase I rather than deferred.
why: Caries control is bundled into Phase I with SRP, since open lesions are hard to instrument and to keep clean.
Caries is not deferred to after surgery; cavitated surfaces hold plaque and undermine Phase I.
Caries control is part of periodontal treatment planning because open lesions trap plaque.
The final RPD comes late in the plan; caries control happens early, in Phase I.

likely.t: Caries control is part of Phase I; the treatment sequence

stem: At which appointment is the final decision about periodontal surgery actually made?
choices: The first scaling and root planing appointment
ex: Re-evaluation shows how well the patient healed and complied — that is when the definitive surgical plan is set, not at the first visit.
why: The Phase I re-evaluation shows healing and compliance, which is when the surgical plan is set.
At the initial exam you don't yet know how the tissue will respond to Phase I.
Maintenance follows active therapy; the surgical decision is made earlier, at re-evaluation.
The first SRP appointment is part of Phase I; its result isn't known until the re-evaluation.

likely.t: Caries control is part of Phase I; the treatment sequence

stem: In the classic Becker et al. data cited in lecture, which group lost teeth at roughly double the rate of patients who kept their maintenance visits?
choices: Treated patients who skipped maintenance visits
Patients who refused periodontal treatment altogether
Treated patients who also took systemic antibiotics
Patients with gingivitis who skipped their recalls
ex: Treated-without-maintenance patients lost about 0.22 teeth/year versus 0.11 teeth/year for treated-with-maintenance patients — roughly double.
why: Treated patients who skipped maintenance lost teeth at about twice the rate of those who kept their recall visits (about 0.22 vs 0.11 teeth a year).
Untreated patients did even worse: they lost roughly three times as many teeth as treated patients, more than the twofold gap.
Antibiotic use wasn't one of the groups compared; the data compared untreated, treated-without-maintenance and maintained patients.
The groups compared were periodontitis patients; the twofold gap is between treated patients with and without maintenance.

likely.t: Maintenance works: the Becker tooth-loss figures

stem: Two patients both have interdental CAL ≥5 mm, bone loss into the middle third of the root, and 7 mm pockets. What moves one of them from Stage 3 to Stage 4?
choices: ≥5 teeth lost to periodontitis, or a need for complex rehabilitation
A vertical bone defect of 3 mm or more on at least one tooth
A bone-loss/age ratio above 1.0 at the worst tooth
Smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day
ex: Stages 3 and 4 share the same CAL (≥5 mm) and bone-loss (middle third or beyond) cutoffs. They are separated by tooth loss to periodontitis (≤4 teeth = Stage 3, ≥5 = Stage 4) and by whether the case needs complex, multidisciplinary rehabilitation (masticatory dysfunction, mobility ≥2, bite collapse, fewer than 20 teeth left). A ≥3 mm vertical defect is a Stage 3 finding; the bone-loss/age ratio and smoking set the grade, not the stage.
why: Stage 4 is set by losing 5 or more teeth to periodontitis or needing complex rehabilitation.
A 3 mm+ vertical defect is a Stage 3 finding; it doesn't separate Stage 3 from Stage 4.
The bone-loss/age ratio sets the grade, not the stage.
Smoking is a grade modifier, so it can't move a case from Stage 3 to Stage 4.

likely.t: Stage 4 complexity factors (the 2018 AAP/EFP tables)

stem: In the 2017 classification, what does grading describe that staging does not?
choices: Its rate of progression and likely response
The current severity and extent of attachment loss
How complex the case will be to manage
Whether the disease is localized or generalized
ex: Staging captures severity at presentation (CAL, bone loss, teeth lost) plus the complexity of management. Grading estimates how fast the disease is moving and how the patient will respond, which is where risk (smoking, HbA1c) enters the diagnosis. Localized vs. generalized is the extent, written in front of the stage.
why: Grading estimates how fast the disease is moving and how the patient will respond, where risk factors enter.
Severity and extent of attachment loss at presentation are what staging captures.
Complexity of management is part of staging, not grading.
Localized vs generalized is the extent, written in front of the stage, not what the grade describes.

stem: Of the six suture materials on the course chart, which is natural and monofilament, resorbs fastest (7–10 days), but handles very poorly?
ex: Chromic gut: natural monofilament, 7–10 day resorption, low strength, mild reaction, very bad handling.
why: Chromic gut is natural, monofilament, resorbs in 7-10 days and handles very badly.
PGA is synthetic and braided, resorbs slowest (55-70 days) and handles great.
Silk is natural but braided and non-resorbable, with great handling.
PTFE is synthetic and non-resorbable, with good handling.

likely.t: The suture materials: resorption, braided vs monofilament, tissue reaction, uses

stem: Which suture material is synthetic and braided, resorbs slowest of the resorbable options (55–70 days), and is used for ridge and sinus augmentation?
ex: PGA: synthetic braided resorbable, 55–70 days, moderate strength, bad tissue reaction, great handling. Silk is the other braided suture, but it's natural and non-resorbable. PGCL is the other synthetic resorbable, but it's a monofilament and resorbs faster (22–55 days). Chromic gut is natural and monofilament, and resorbs fastest (7–10 days).
why: PGA is synthetic, braided and resorbs over 55-70 days, so it suits ridge and sinus augmentation.
Silk is braided too, but it is natural and non-resorbable.
PGCL is synthetic and resorbable, but it is a monofilament that resorbs faster (22-55 days).
Chromic gut is natural and monofilament, and it resorbs fastest (7-10 days).

likely.t: The suture materials: resorption, braided vs monofilament, tissue reaction, uses

cue: "Poly-Propylene is Plain like nylon": no tissue adherence. PTFE is the pricey all-rounder.
stem: Which non-resorbable suture is described as having no adherence to tissue, similar to nylon?
ex: Poly-propylene is the non-resorbable monofilament that behaves like nylon: no adherence to tissue. PTFE is the look-alike trap here: it is also a synthetic non-resorbable monofilament, but the lecture tags it as the high-cost option used in every surgery type except pure soft-tissue grafting, not the "like nylon" one. Silk is non-resorbable too, but it is natural and braided, the opposite of a nylon-like monofilament.
why: Poly-propylene is the non-resorbable monofilament with no adherence to tissue, similar to nylon.
Silk is non-resorbable but natural and braided, and its tissue reaction is very bad.
PTFE is also a non-resorbable monofilament, but it is tagged as the high-cost option for all surgeries except pure soft-tissue grafting.
PGCL is resorbable (22-55 days), so it isn't a non-resorbable suture.

likely.t: The suture materials: resorption, braided vs monofilament, tissue reaction, uses

stem: Which material causes the worst tissue reaction of all six sutures taught, despite handling very well?
ex: Silk: natural braided non-resorbable, high strength, very bad tissue reaction, great handling — and must be removed at 7 days.
why: Silk has the worst tissue reaction (very bad) of the six, despite great handling.
PGCL has a great (minimal) tissue reaction.
PTFE has a great (minimal) tissue reaction.
Chromic gut's tissue reaction is only mild; its weakness is very bad handling.

likely.t: The suture materials: resorption, braided vs monofilament, tissue reaction, uses

stem: Which natural, braided, non-resorbable suture on the course chart must be physically removed, and when?
ex: Silk is natural, braided and non-resorbable, and the course chart says to remove it at 7 days, earlier than the 10-14 days the notes give for non-absorbables in general. Its braid traps plaque, which is behind its very bad tissue reaction.
why: Silk is the chart's natural, braided non-resorbable, and the chart says to remove it at 7 days.
PTFE is non-resorbable, but it is a synthetic monofilament, and the 7-day removal is noted for silk.
Poly-propylene is non-resorbable and does come out, but it is a synthetic monofilament, not the natural, braided suture the stem describes; that one is silk, out at 7 days.
Silk is the right material, but the chart singles it out for removal at 7 days; 10-14 days is the general window for non-absorbables.

likely.t: The suture materials: resorption, braided vs monofilament, tissue reaction, uses

cue: "Silk and PGA wear braids"; gut and PTFE are single strands. Natural: gut and silk (from animals). Synthetic: PGA and PTFE.
stem: Match each suture material to its construction.
ex: Only silk and PGA are braided; gut and PTFE are monofilament. Origin splits the other way: gut and silk are natural, PGA and PTFE synthetic.

likely.t: The suture materials: resorption, braided vs monofilament, tissue reaction, uses

stem: In suture sizing, what does a larger number mean, and what does that require?
ex: Suture sizes run backwards: a bigger number (5-0 vs 3-0) is a thinner strand. Thinner material slips more easily, so it needs more throws to hold the knot.
why: Sizes run backwards: a bigger number is a thinner strand, and thinner material needs more throws to hold.
A larger number means a smaller diameter, not a larger one.
A larger number is a thinner strand; it does need more knots, but it isn't thicker.
A larger number is thinner, but thinner material slips more, so it needs more knots, not fewer.

stem: Which flap design offers limited access and is difficult to advance because of lateral attachment, making it best for minor augmentation or simple implant placement?
ex: A sulcular flap has no vertical release, so the tissue stays attached on both sides. That limits access and makes it hard to advance, which is fine for minor augmentation or a single implant. When more access is needed, one vertical (pyramidal) or two (trapezoidal) are added.
why: A sulcular flap has no vertical release, so it stays attached laterally: limited access, hard to advance.
A trapezoidal flap has two vertical releases, giving wide access and easy coronal advancement.
A pyramidal flap adds one vertical release, giving more access than a sulcular flap, as for an implant with an onlay graft.
An envelope flap lifts only buccal tissue to tuck a soft-tissue graft for root coverage; it isn't the minor-augmentation or implant flap.

stem: What is a partial-thickness flap?
choices: A split-thickness flap, with the periosteum left on the bone
A full-thickness flap reflected only partway to the vestibule
A pyramidal flap, with a vertical release on one side only
An envelope flap, with the papillae left unreflected
ex: On the exam, "partial thickness" and "split thickness" mean the same thing (Dr. Abou-Arraj, Nov 12): the periosteum is left on the bone and only mucosa and submucosa are reflected, the bed a soft-tissue graft needs. A full-thickness (mucoperiosteal) flap takes the periosteum with it and exposes bone, however far it is reflected.
why: Partial and split thickness mean the same thing: the periosteum stays on the bone and only mucosa and submucosa are reflected.
How far a flap is lifted doesn't make it partial; a flap that takes the periosteum is full thickness (mucoperiosteal) and exposes bone.
Pyramidal names the outline (one vertical release); thickness is a separate axis of flap design.
Envelope names the outline (buccal only, papillae intact), not whether the periosteum is lifted.

likely.t: Full vs partial (split) thickness: which procedures need each

cue: Partial = split: the periosteum stays on the bone.

stem: Why must the base of a flap be at least as wide as its free edge?
choices: To protect the flap's blood supply
To keep the free edge from inverting at closure
To keep the verticals at the line angles
To avoid lifting the periosteum with the flap
ex: Once a flap is reflected, its only blood supply enters through its base. If the base is narrower than the free edge, the far end is starved of blood and can necrose. Line-angle placement and full vs partial thickness are separate decisions.
why: Once the flap is reflected its only blood supply enters through the base, so a narrow base starves the free edge.
Margin inversion is a closure issue (what a horizontal mattress prevents), not what base width is about.
Line-angle placement is its own principle, protecting the papilla and avoiding recession, not a reason for base width.
Whether periosteum is lifted is the full vs partial thickness choice; base width is about blood supply.

likely.t: A flap's base must be wider than its free edge

stem: A surgeon makes the same incision around tooth #8, which is present, and continues it along the edentulous ridge where #9 used to be. What are the two parts of that incision called?
choices: Intrasulcular at #8, crestal at #9 — same technique, named by tooth presence
Crestal at #8, intrasulcular at #9 — named by where the scalpel blade enters
Both are called vertical incisions, since each runs along the long axis
Both are called pouch incisions, since neither releases the flap laterally
ex: Intrasulcular and crestal are the same physical incision. The name changes based only on whether a tooth is present at that site, not on any difference in technique.
why: Same incision: intrasulcular where a tooth is present (#8), crestal along the edentulous ridge (#9).
This reverses them: crestal is the edentulous-ridge name and intrasulcular the name around a tooth.
Vertical incisions are releasing cuts running apically, not ones that follow the sulcus or crest.
Pouch describes a flap design; the incisions themselves are named intrasulcular and crestal.

stem: Why would a surgeon drop a vertical incision instead of just extending the intrasulcular incision to more teeth?
choices: To gain apical exposure without involving teeth that don't need it
To keep the incision line directly over the bony defect
To avoid lifting the periosteum, keeping the flap split thickness
Because vertical incisions heal faster than intrasulcular ones
ex: When an intrasulcular or crestal incision alone doesn't give enough exposure, a vertical release at the line angle opens the flap apically, so you reach bone and defects without including teeth you don't need, which would compromise esthetics for no benefit. It doesn't change flap thickness, and it stays away from the defect itself.
why: A vertical release opens the flap apically for access, without dragging extra, uninvolved teeth into the horizontal incision.
Incisions are kept at a distance from the bony defect, never directly over it; that is one of the five principles.
A vertical release doesn't change flap thickness; the verticals of a major augmentation flap are full thickness.
Vertical incisions aren't chosen for faster healing; they're added purely for access.

stem: A root-coverage case needs a soft-tissue graft placed without disturbing the papillae at all. Which flap design fits?
ex: The envelope/pouch flap elevates only the buccal tissue and never reflects the papillae — exactly what a root-coverage graft needs.
why: The envelope (pouch) flap elevates only buccal tissue and never reflects the papillae.
A trapezoidal flap uses two vertical releases and reflects tissue widely, disturbing the area.
A soft-tissue graft needs a split-thickness bed for blood supply, and exposing bone doesn't spare papillae.
Extending a sulcular flap across 4 teeth reflects the papillae along the way.

cue: Trapezoid = two releases, a door on each side, so the flap slides up with no tension.
stem: A major vertical ridge-augmentation graft needs the flap to advance coronally with zero tension over the graft. Which flap design is built for that?
ex: Two releasing incisions, one on each side of the defect, let the flap stretch coronally without tension — a single vertical often can't reach that far without tearing.
why: Two releasing incisions let the trapezoidal flap advance coronally with tension-free closure over a big graft.
A sulcular flap has no release and is hard to advance, fine only for minor augmentation.
A pyramidal flap has only one release, often not enough reach for a major vertical graft.
An envelope flap has no vertical release and doesn't advance far.

stem: An implant needs onlay bone grafting around it, and the surgeon wants more access than a sulcular flap gives without opening both sides of the site. What's the fit?
ex: A pyramidal flap uses one vertical plus an intrasulcular incision across three teeth. It gives more exposure than a sulcular flap without the second release a trapezoidal flap needs, which is reserved for major augmentation. An envelope flap has no vertical release at all, and bone grafting needs a full-thickness flap, not a split-thickness one.
why: A pyramidal flap's single vertical release gives more access than a sulcular flap without opening both sides.
A trapezoidal flap opens both sides with two releases, reserved for major augmentation.
An envelope flap has no vertical release, so it gives even less access than needed here.
Bone grafting needs bone exposed, which means a full-thickness flap, not split thickness.

cue: Sub-marginal = "cut it off": the incision sits below the margin and the strip of pocket wall is thrown away.
stem: A site probes 6 mm and needs its pocket surgically eliminated rather than the pocket wall reflected and repositioned. Which incision is designed for exactly this?
ex: Placed below the free gingival margin and excisional by design — a strip of pocket wall is cut away and discarded, not reflected back, leaving a shallower sulcus.
why: A sub-marginal incision sits below the gingival margin and cuts away a strip of pocket wall to eliminate the pocket.
An intrasulcular incision keeps the pocket wall and reflects it, rather than removing it.
A crestal incision is the same cut on an edentulous ridge; it doesn't remove pocket wall.
A vertical incision only releases the flap for access; it doesn't remove pocket tissue.

likely.t: The sub-marginal incision

stem: Why does a sub-marginal incision leave recession, and when is that acceptable?
choices: Pocket wall is cut away on purpose; right for a deep pocket, never for a recession site
The flap is repositioned too far apically by mistake; it's a technique error to avoid
Pocket wall is cut away on purpose; it's also the incision of choice to treat recession
The tissue is only reflected, so the margin rebounds to its old level within weeks
ex: A sub-marginal incision is excisional: it sits below the free gingival margin, and the strip of pocket wall coronal to it is removed (for example, about 3 mm off a 6 mm pocket), leaving a shallower, cleansable sulcus. The recession it leaves is the goal when pocket depth is the problem. The trap is using it on a recession site: never; recession calls for a graft.
why: The pocket wall coronal to the incision is excised on purpose, so the recession is intended: right for a deep pocket, never used where recession is the problem.
Nothing is repositioned by mistake: the tissue coronal to the incision is removed deliberately, so the recession isn't an error.
It does cut pocket wall away on purpose, which is exactly why it is never used on a site treated for recession; thin or receded tissue calls for grafting.
The tissue isn't reflected and replaced; it is excised, so the margin doesn't rebound.

likely.t: The sub-marginal incision

stem: A soft-tissue graft is being placed to thicken keratinized tissue around a tooth. What flap thickness is reflected at the recipient site, and why?
choices: Partial thickness, leaving the periosteum as a vascular bed for the graft
Full thickness, so the graft can attach directly to the exposed bone
Partial thickness, leaving the epithelium in place for the graft to fuse to
Full thickness, because periosteum left on the bone would reject the graft
ex: On the exam, partial thickness and split thickness mean the same thing: the periosteum is left on the bone. A soft-tissue graft's recipient site is prepared this way so the graft's blood vessels can anastomose with the bed's. Full thickness is for procedures whose goal is bone (implants, augmentation, crown lengthening with osseous surgery).
why: Partial (split) thickness leaves the periosteum on the bone, a vascularized bed whose vessels anastomose with the graft's.
A soft-tissue graft needs a blood supply from below; bare bone doesn't give one, so full thickness is for bone work.
Partial thickness is right, but a graft fuses only to cut, epithelium-free surfaces; intact epithelium keeps the vessels from joining.
Periosteum doesn't reject a graft; it is the vascular bed that feeds it.

likely.t: Full vs partial (split) thickness: which procedures need each

stem: Harvesting a palatal connective tissue graft, which donor site is preferred and why?
choices: The molar area: less fatty tissue, so the graft shrinks less
The premolar area: thinner tissue that is easier to suture
The molar area: its thicker epithelium gives a bulkier graft
The premolar area: more adipose tissue to add bulk
ex: Harvest from the molar area: the premolar region has proportionally more adipose tissue under the epithelium, and fat resorbs quickly once transplanted, so a graft with too much of it visibly shrinks. The tempting trap is calling fat useful bulk. Watch for the greater palatine artery during any palatal harvest.
why: The premolar region carries more fatty adipose tissue, which resorbs once transplanted, so molar-area grafts shrink less.
Premolar tissue isn't preferred: it carries more adipose, and that fat resorbs and shrinks the graft.
The molar area is right, but not for its epithelium: a connective tissue graft has its epithelium trimmed away.
Adipose isn't useful bulk: it resorbs quickly once transplanted, which is why the premolar area is avoided.

stem: Why is a braided suture generally avoided in favor of a monofilament, even though silk (braided) is still used for some cases?
answer: A braided suture's woven strands wick and trap bacteria the way a smooth monofilament strand doesn't, which is the mechanism behind silk's very bad tissue-reaction score. Silk is still used, for osseous surgery and crown lengthening, because it handles beautifully, and it comes out early, at 7 days.
ex: If a braided suture must be removed, wipe it with chlorhexidine gauze first so plaque trapped in the weave doesn't get dragged into the flap on the way out.

stem: A patient with thin buccal tissue on the lower incisors is about to start orthodontic treatment that will push those teeth further buccally. What's the recommended sequence?
choices: Graft to thicken the tissue prophylactically before orthodontic movement begins
Start orthodontics and graft only if recession actually develops
Delay orthodontics indefinitely — thin tissue is a permanent contraindication
Graft after orthodontics is finished, regardless of what happens during treatment
ex: This is periodontal-orthodontic clearance: grafting ahead of the movement prevents the recession that pushing a tooth through thin tissue tends to cause, rather than treating it after the fact.
why: Thickening the tissue before moving the teeth prevents recession that pushing them through thin tissue tends to cause.
Waiting for recession means treating damage that grafting first would have prevented.
Thin tissue isn't a permanent contraindication; grafting first allows orthodontics to proceed.
Grafting after orthodontics misses the window; the recession risk is during the movement.

stem: Which of the prognosis systems can be used as a diagnostic prognosis?
ex: Only McGuire & Nunn can be diagnostic: a forecast of what happens if the patient takes no treatment. All three systems can be therapeutic. Kwok & Caton can't be diagnostic because it asks whether periodontal stability can be achieved with treatment, which is also why questionable sits in its middle.
why: McGuire & Nunn is the only system that can be diagnostic (the outcome with no treatment); it can be therapeutic too.
Kwok & Caton asks whether stability can be achieved with treatment, so it can only ever be therapeutic.
Kwok & Caton judges the outcome of treatment, so it is therapeutic only; only McGuire & Nunn adds a diagnostic version.
All three can be therapeutic, but only McGuire & Nunn can be diagnostic; 'all three' belongs to the therapeutic question.

likely.t: Diagnostic vs therapeutic: only McGuire & Nunn works diagnostically

cue: McGuire & Nunn = "Maintain" (M for M). Miller & McEntire = Molars retained. Kwok & Caton = Can it be stabilized?
stem: What does the McGuire & Nunn system assess?
choices: How easy the tooth is to maintain in the mouth
A numeric score of how likely a molar is to be retained
ex: McGuire & Nunn asks whether a tooth can be maintained (kept in the mouth) and how much effort that will take (good: easy to maintain; poor: kept only with significant effort). A numeric score of how likely a molar is to be retained is Miller & McEntire: molars only, quantitative. "Likelihood of stability" is Kwok & Caton, and the rate of progression is what grading describes.
why: McGuire & Nunn asks how easy the tooth will be to maintain.
That is Miller & McEntire: molars only, scored as a number. McGuire & Nunn rates any tooth by how easy it will be to keep.
Likelihood of periodontal stability is what Kwok & Caton assesses.
Rate of progression is what grading describes, not a prognosis system.

likely.t: McGuire & Nunn rates retention (maintainability); about 80% / 50% accurate

cue: Kwok & Caton looks at the Whole mouth only; McGuire & Nunn can rate each tooth (or the whole mouth); Miller & McEntire only molars.
stem: Which of the three prognosis systems is given for the whole dentition, not tooth by tooth?
ex: Kwok & Caton is the whole-dentition system: it asks whether periodontal stability can be reached with treatment. McGuire & Nunn can be given for the whole dentition too, but it is also given tooth by tooth, and Miller & McEntire scores single molars.
why: Kwok & Caton judges the whole dentition: can periodontal stability be reached with treatment?
McGuire & Nunn can be given for the whole dentition, but it is also given tooth by tooth.
Miller & McEntire scores single molars.
Only Kwok & Caton works at the whole-dentition level alone; McGuire & Nunn is also given per tooth, and Miller & McEntire per molar.

likely.t: Kwok & Caton: stability, the whole dentition, therapeutic only, its categories

stem: What does P4 stand for in "P4 medicine", as the lecture defines it?
ex: P4 medicine is personalized, preventive, predictive and participatory: estimate risk, personalize it to the patient's own risk markers and make the patient a participant in their care. Applied to periodontics, the lecture adds a fifth P, periodontal (P5). Prophylactic, proactive and progressive aren't among them, and periodontal belongs to P5, not P4.
why: P4 is Personalized, Preventive, Predictive, Participatory; periodontal care adds Periodontal for P5.
Prophylactic and Progressive aren't among the four Ps; Personalized and Predictive are.
Proactive isn't one of the Ps, and Periodontal is the fifth P, added for P5.
Personalized and Participatory are missing; Periodontal and Prophylactic aren't in P4.

cue: "72% just wanted a cleaning": that's why every new patient gets a full perio exam.
stem: About what share of patients later diagnosed with periodontitis originally presented saying they just wanted a routine cleaning?
ex: About 72% of patients later diagnosed with periodontitis first came in asking only for a cleaning, which is why every new patient needs a full periodontal exam.
why: About 72% of patients later diagnosed with periodontitis first asked only for a routine cleaning.
About 42% (42.5%) is the share of US adults over 30 with periodontitis, a different statistic.
25% is far too low; the point was that most patients, about 72%, had no idea anything was wrong.
95% is the D1110 share among 50-64-year-olds, a different statistic.

stem: D1110 (prophylaxis) makes up 95.4% of cleaning codes in patients aged 50 to 64. What makes this figure notable?
choices: It climbs with age, though rising disease prevalence says it should fall
It matches the periodontitis prevalence expected in that age group
It is lower than the prophylaxis share in patients aged 19 to 34
It shows periodontitis becomes less common after about age 50
ex: D1110 share climbs steadily with age (72.3% at 19-34, 87.5% at 35-49, 95.4% at 50-64) even though periodontitis becomes more common with age — evidence of under-diagnosis or under-escalation, not less disease.
why: Periodontitis becomes more common with age, so the prophylaxis share should fall; instead it climbs to 95.4%, pointing to under-diagnosis.
It runs opposite to the epidemiology: periodontitis prevalence rises with age while the prophylaxis share climbs.
The 19-34 share is lower (72.3%); the share climbs with age, to 87.5% at 35-49 and 95.4% at 50-64.
Periodontitis becomes more common with age (70.1% of adults 65 and older), which is what makes the climbing D1110 share a mismatch.

cue: PISA: a ~34 mm² scratch in health vs a ~2,300 mm² open wound in perio, 60-70 times bigger.
stem: Roughly how much larger is the periodontal inflamed surface area (PISA) in a patient with mild-to-moderate periodontitis compared to a periodontally healthy patient?
choices: About 60-70 times larger: about 2,309 mm² vs 34 mm²
About twice as large: about 70 mm² vs 34 mm²
About 10 times larger: about 340 mm² vs 34 mm²
About the same: healthy sulci are lined with inflamed epithelium too
ex: Mild-to-moderate periodontitis gives an inflamed pocket surface of roughly 2,309 mm², against about 34 mm² in health: an open wound around 60–70 times larger.
why: Mild-to-moderate periodontitis inflames about 2,309 mm² of pocket surface vs about 34 mm² in health, roughly 60-70x.
Twice as large badly understates it; the inflamed area is about 2,309 mm².
Ten times is still far too small; the inflamed area is about 2,309 mm², near 60-70x.
A healthy sulcus isn't inflamed; PISA counts only inflamed pocket surface, about 34 mm² in health (a small paper cut).

stem: What does PISA stand for and what does it estimate?
answer: Periodontal Inflamed Surface Area — the total area of pocket epithelium facing active inflammation, used to illustrate how large an inflammatory burden periodontitis represents systemically.

cue: Summed 0-4 scores = UniFe ("Unified" into one number); PRA is the hexagon picture.
stem: Which whole-patient risk tool scores smoking (cigarettes a day), diabetic status (HbA1c), the number of pockets ≥5 mm, BOP % and the bone-loss/age ratio, each 0-4, and sums them into one risk score?
ex: UniFe (Trombelli et al.) sums five 0-4 scores (cigarettes a day, HbA1c, pockets ≥5 mm, BOP % and bone loss/age) into a five-tier risk score from low to high. The PRA is drawn as a spider-web plot, and PreViser/PAT gives its own risk score, which agreed fairly well with UniFe head to head.
why: UniFe sums five 0-4 scores (cigarettes a day, HbA1c, pockets ≥5 mm, BOP %, bone loss/age) into a five-tier risk score.
The PRA (Lang & Tonetti) plots its factors on a spider-web diagram; five 0-4 items summed into one score are UniFe's.
PreViser/PAT (Page et al.) also combines clinical, radiographic and behavioral inputs into a risk tier, but the five summed 0-4 items are UniFe's.
Miller & McEntire is a molar prognosis system, not a whole-patient summed risk score.

stem: Per the risk-stratified maintenance protocol, how often should a low-risk patient get professional biofilm/calculus removal?
ex: In the risk-stratified protocol, low-risk patients get biofilm/calculus removal every 6 months. Moderate risk is every 4–6 months and high risk every 2–4 months.
why: Low-risk patients get biofilm and calculus removal every 6 months.
Every 3 months is too frequent for low risk; high risk is every 2-4 months.
Every 2-4 months is the high-risk interval.
Every 4-6 months is the moderate-risk interval.

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

stem: Per the risk-stratified maintenance protocol, how often should a high-risk patient get an oral exam/periodontal screening (separate from the comprehensive exam)?
choices: Screening is not scheduled separately for high-risk patients
ex: High-risk patients get a separate screening every 3 months on top of the 6–12-month comprehensive exam. Moderate risk is every 6 months, and low risk has no separate screening.
why: High-risk patients get a separate screening every 3 months, on top of the comprehensive exam.
Every 6 months is the moderate-risk screening interval.
Every 12 months is the outer limit of the comprehensive exam, not the high-risk screening.
High-risk patients do get a separate screening; it's low-risk patients who don't.

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

stem: Why is a periodontally treated maintenance patient with every site reading 3 mm not automatically a candidate for a plain prophylaxis?
choices: Healing left a long junctional epithelium, which breaks down more easily
A 3 mm reading after periodontal therapy is too unreliable to trust
Insurance won't reimburse a prophylaxis once perio therapy is done
Treated sites heal with new connective tissue that is still immature
ex: After treatment the pocket is lined by a long junctional epithelium, not a new connective-tissue attachment. It breaks down more easily under inflammation, so a treated patient stays on periodontal maintenance even when every site reads 3 mm.
why: Treated pockets heal with a long junctional epithelium, which breaks down under inflammation more easily than a connective-tissue attachment with a short junctional epithelium.
The 3 mm reading can be accurate; what differs is the attachment under it.
The reason is biological, not billing: the healed attachment is structurally weaker, so the maintenance code and protocol still apply.
Treatment doesn't rebuild a connective-tissue attachment here; the pocket heals with a long junctional epithelium, the weaker seal.

stem: Why does periodontal maintenance land on roughly a 3-month interval for most patients?
answer: Pathogenic subgingival species begin re-establishing 4-8 weeks after treatment, and by about 9-11 weeks the subgingival microbiome can repopulate close to pre-treatment levels — a 3-month recall sits inside that recolonization window.

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

stem: Why are patients undergoing active orthodontic tooth movement typically seen for periodontal maintenance every 4-6 weeks rather than every 3 months?
choices: Inflammation during tooth movement can uncouple bone formation from resorption
Orthodontic brackets make 3-month scheduling physically impossible
Orthodontic force causes bone loss on its own, whatever the biofilm control
It matches a fixed insurance billing cycle for patients in braces
ex: During active tooth movement, inflammation can tip remodeling toward resorption and cause real bone loss, so biofilm is controlled more tightly, every 4–6 weeks.
why: Inflammation during active tooth movement can tip remodeling toward resorption and cause real bone loss, so biofilm is controlled every 4-6 weeks.
Brackets don't make 3-month visits impossible; the visits do line up with appliance adjustments, but the shorter interval is about bone risk.
Tooth movement remodels bone; the loss comes when inflammation uncouples formation from resorption, which is why tight biofilm control is the point.
The interval comes from biology (bone remodeling), not insurance cycles.

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

stem: What is the number one reason patients decline a periodontal treatment plan, per the lecture's patient-trust data?
choices: The cost of the treatment plan
ex: The number one reason patients decline a periodontal treatment plan is that they don't trust their dental provider: 62% delay treatment, switch providers, seek a second opinion or refuse care because they disagree with or distrust the diagnosis. Cost is rarely the real barrier; it becomes an objection when patients feel rushed, can't ask questions, sense disagreement in the team or aren't offered ways to manage it. The hygienist is the most trusted person in the office.
why: Lack of trust is the top reason: 62% delay, switch, seek a second opinion or refuse because they distrust the diagnosis.
Cost is rarely the real barrier (patients said they'd pay about $633 a tooth to keep it); it becomes one when they feel rushed or unheard.
Fear of pain wasn't the top reason in the lecture's data; distrust of the provider or the diagnosis was.
Time wasn't the top reason either; distrust was, which is why the whole team needs one consistent message.

stem: Match each part of the risk-stratified protocol to its interval.
pairs: Covered by the 6-12 month comprehensive exam
ex: Risk sets the intervals. Low risk relies on the 6-12 month comprehensive exam with no separate screening; moderate risk adds a screening every 6 months and high risk every 3 months. High-risk patients also get biofilm/calculus removal and subgingival debridement every 2-4 months (moderate every 4-6, low every 6).

likely.t: Risk-stratified maintenance intervals

stem: In the McGuire & Nunn system, what actually decides which prognosis category a tooth lands in?
choices: How well the tooth can be maintained in the mouth
How likely the tooth is to show disease progression
How likely the tooth is to become mobile without treatment
How often treatment will need to be redone
ex: Most of the class picked disease progression in the in-class poll. The driving factor is maintainability: how hard it will be to keep the tooth. That is what separates McGuire & Nunn from Kwok & Caton, which asks about periodontal stability.

Disease progression was the class's favorite pick, but the system is based on maintainability.
Mobility is one input, but the category reflects overall maintainability, not mobility alone.
Retreatment frequency isn't what the categories sort by; maintainability is.

likely.t: McGuire & Nunn rates retention (maintainability); about 80% / 50% accurate

stem: Put the McGuire & Nunn prognosis categories in order, best to worst.
ex: Flagged in class as a high-likelihood midterm question. Everyone wants to swap poor and questionable. Questionable sits right before hopeless because the system sorts teeth by whether they can be kept.

likely.t: McGuire & Nunn order: good, fair, poor, questionable, hopeless

stem: Why does 'questionable' come after 'poor' (right before hopeless) in McGuire & Nunn?
choices: It sorts by whether a tooth can be kept, and a questionable tooth won't stay put: it worsens to hopeless or improves to poor
Questionable teeth always have more attachment loss and mobility than poor teeth, so the list simply runs from least to most destroyed, with hopeless last
It mirrors Kwok & Caton, where questionable also sits right before hopeless, so the two scales line up
Questionable is a category used only for molars, so it is placed last as a separate molar-only group
ex: McGuire & Nunn sorts teeth by whether they can be kept. A poor tooth (attachment loss, Class II furcation, mobility) can be kept with significant effort; a questionable tooth is one we genuinely question keeping, and it doesn't stay there: it gets worse and becomes hopeless, or improves and moves up to poor. Questionable isn't defined by more destruction than poor, which is why everyone wants to swap the two.
why: Categories sort by whether a tooth can be kept, and a questionable tooth won't stay put: it worsens or improves.
Questionable isn't defined by having more destruction than poor; it reflects doubt that the tooth will stay.
In Kwok & Caton questionable sits in the middle (we don't know if stability is achievable); only McGuire & Nunn puts it right before hopeless.

likely.t: McGuire & Nunn order: good, fair, poor, questionable, hopeless

stem: If teeth with a 'good' prognosis are removed from the analysis, how often does a McGuire & Nunn prognosis turn out right?
ex: Once the easy "good" teeth are excluded, McGuire & Nunn predictions are right only about half the time, no better than a coin flip. Prognosis is a guide, not a promise.
why: Without the easy 'good' teeth, predictions are right only about half the time, a coin flip.

95% is far too high; even overall accuracy is about 80%.
20% is too low; it is about 50%, a coin flip.

likely.t: McGuire & Nunn rates retention (maintainability); about 80% / 50% accurate

stem: Longitudinally, what happens to teeth given a hopeless prognosis in patients who stay well maintained?
choices: They are often kept significantly longer than predicted
They almost always exfoliate within a year
They must be extracted before maintenance can start
They cause the neighboring teeth to fail
ex: In well-maintained patients even hopeless teeth are often kept much longer than predicted: on average teeth do better than their prognosis, and most teeth leave the mouth because a dentist extracts them, not because they exfoliate (unlike implants). The exceptions are smokers and patients with very poor hygiene, and even very poor hygiene tracks the prediction when those patients keep up with maintenance.
why: In well-maintained patients, hopeless teeth are often kept much longer than predicted.
They rarely exfoliate; most teeth leave because a dentist extracts them.
They don't have to be extracted before maintenance; many are kept in maintenance for years.
That isn't what the longitudinal data showed; the point was that they last longer than expected.

likely.t: McGuire & Nunn rates retention (maintainability); about 80% / 50% accurate

cue: Diagnostic prognosis = the "Do nothing" forecast. Therapeutic = the "with Treatment" forecast.
stem: What is a diagnostic prognosis?
choices: The expected outcome if the patient receives no treatment
The expected outcome after the recommended treatment
A prognosis assigned only to molars
A prognosis assigned only at maintenance visits
ex: Diagnostic: you make the diagnosis and the patient walks out untreated. Therapeutic: you recommend treatment and predict how it changes the outcome, which is a useful way to show a patient what treatment buys them.
why: A diagnostic prognosis predicts the outcome if the patient walks out untreated.
The expected outcome after recommended treatment is a therapeutic prognosis.
Molar-only describes Miller & McEntire, not the diagnostic vs therapeutic distinction.
It isn't tied to maintenance visits; it's the no-treatment prediction.

likely.t: Diagnostic vs therapeutic: only McGuire & Nunn works diagnostically

stem: Why does 'questionable' sit in the middle of the Kwok & Caton scale instead of right before hopeless?
choices: It asks whether stability is likely, unknown or unlikely with treatment
It asks how much effort each tooth will take to keep in the mouth
Its categories are ranked by the deepest probing depth in the mouth
Questionable is its only category that can be used diagnostically
ex: Kwok & Caton asks whether periodontal stability (arrested attachment loss) can be achieved with treatment: likely (favorable), don't know (questionable) or unlikely (unfavorable), so questionable falls in the middle. McGuire & Nunn sorts teeth by whether they can be maintained, which is why its questionable comes right before hopeless. Remember what each system is based on, not just the two orders.
why: Kwok & Caton asks whether periodontal stability can be achieved with treatment: likely, don't know or unlikely, so questionable (don't know) falls in the middle.
How much effort a tooth takes to keep is McGuire & Nunn's question, which is why its questionable sits right before hopeless.
It isn't ordered by probing depth; it's ordered by how likely stability is with treatment.
Kwok & Caton is therapeutic only, so none of its categories is diagnostic.

likely.t: Kwok & Caton: stability, the whole dentition, therapeutic only, its categories

stem: For which patient would Kwok & Caton be the more useful prognosis system?
choices: A medically complex patient who smokes and has a high A1c
A patient who asks what happens if they take no treatment
A single mandibular molar with a Class II furcation
A healthy nonsmoker with no systemic risk factors

That makes it the better choice for a medically complex patient. A no-treatment forecast is diagnostic, which only McGuire & Nunn can give.
why: Kwok & Caton judges stability with treatment, so smoking cessation and getting the A1c under control become part of the plan it rates.
A no-treatment forecast is a diagnostic prognosis, which only McGuire & Nunn can give.
A single tooth calls for a per-tooth prognosis such as McGuire & Nunn; Kwok & Caton judges the whole dentition.

likely.t: Kwok & Caton: stability, the whole dentition, therapeutic only, its categories

cue: Horizontal bone loss and furcations rarely regenerate, so Kwok & Caton shrugs: Questionable.
stem: In-class case: 78-year-old, ASA II, generalized Stage 3 Grade B periodontitis, mostly horizontal bone loss with furcation involvement. Which Kwok & Caton prognosis fits her?
ex: Horizontal bone loss and furcations are hard to regenerate, so if that is the stage-defining lesion, it is unclear whether stability can be achieved.

Unfavorable would mean stability is unlikely; the case was judged uncertain, not unlikely.

stem: Why did the class recommend returning the 78-year-old Stage 3 patient every 3 months?
choices: Subgingival repopulation takes about 9-11 weeks, and a periodontitis patient stays higher-risk even once healthy
Every patient over 75 needs 3-month recalls regardless of their periodontal diagnosis or risk
The PRA placed the patient in the extraction range, so the 3-month recalls just track the remaining teeth until they are removed
Insurance covers four visits a year, so the interval is set by the coverage rather than by biology

Age and insurance coverage don't set the interval.
why: Subgingival bacteria repopulate in about 9-11 weeks, and a treated periodontitis patient stays higher risk.

cue: Graft + membrane in a narrow vertical defect ≈ three-quarters fill (70-75%).
stem: With a bone replacement graft plus a membrane, roughly how much bone fill is expected in a deep, narrow vertical defect?
ex: A bone graft plus a membrane (maybe with a biologic) gives roughly 70-75% fill in a deep, narrow vertical defect, and young patients heal better. That's why the 13-year-old's involved teeth got a fair, not hopeless, therapeutic prognosis. Horizontal bone loss and furcations, by contrast, are hard to regenerate.

10-20% is far too low for a graft plus membrane in a favorable defect.

cue: Young, few teeth, regenerable defects: treatment turns it into Good to Fair.
stem: In-class case: 13-year-old with localized vertical defects on first molars (molar-incisor pattern, Grade C). What overall therapeutic McGuire & Nunn prognosis fits once regeneration is planned?
choices: Good to fair, with the involved teeth fair
Hopeless for the involved molars, good elsewhere
Poor to questionable, with the involved teeth questionable
Questionable for every tooth until re-evaluation

Her diagnostic prognosis (no treatment) would be poor to questionable: the tempting wrong pick, and the argument for treating.

cue: Neutrophils are "the marines": when they can't find the fight (chemotactic defect), the first teeth in, first molars and incisors, fall first.
stem: About 70% of patients with circumpubertal, molar-incisor-pattern periodontitis have which underlying problem?
ex: About 70% of circumpubertal, molar-incisor-pattern patients have a neutrophil chemotactic deficiency. Neutrophils arrive first ("the marines of your immune system"), so when they can't find the fight, the first teeth to erupt, the first molars and incisors, are hit hardest. Don't mix it up with the other 70%: nicotine use among those whose disease generalizes.

cue: Stage is a scar, not a score: it only goes down if you rebuild the lesion that raised it (regenerate the vertical defect or furcation).

When they quit smoking, since smoking status is part of the staging criteria
After a full year of 3-month maintenance visits with no new attachment loss recorded at any site

stem: What does the Periodontal Risk Assessment (PRA) tool look like?

stem: A site probes 2 mm with 5 mm of gingival recession. What is the clinical attachment level?
ex: CAL = probing depth + recession = 2 + 5 = 7 mm. This slide example is paired with a 7 mm pocket and no recession, which also gives CAL 7 mm: same attachment loss, very different pockets.

stem: Gingival recession is measured from where to where?
choices: Gingival margin to the base of the pocket
CEJ to the base of the pocket

stem: How many probing readings are recorded per tooth?

Four (M, D, B, L), recording the average of the readings at each of the four surfaces

stem: How should the probe be angled when probing interproximally?
choices: Tilted slightly toward the area apical to the contact
Held vertical and stopped at the line angle
Tilted away from the contact, toward the facial surface

cue: Miller mobility: Class 1 under 1 mm, Class 2 between 1 and 2 mm, Class 3 "goes up and down" (vertical). Just past 1 mm is already Class 2.
stem: A tooth moves more than 1 mm but less than 2 mm, with no vertical displacement. What is its Miller mobility class?
ex: Miller Class 1 is under 1 mm, Class 2 is more than 1 mm but under 2 mm, and Class 3 adds vertical displacement. This tooth moves 1–2 mm with no vertical movement, so it is Class 2. The class number isn't the millimeters: Class 1 stops at 1 mm, so anything past 1 mm is already Class 2.
why: More than 1 mm but under 2 mm, with no vertical movement, is Miller Class 2.
Class 1 is movement under 1 mm; this tooth already moves more than 1 mm.
Class 3 requires vertical displacement (a depressible tooth), which is absent here.
Class 0 is physiologic mobility only, not over 1 mm of movement.

stem: What defines Miller Class 3 mobility?
choices: Severe faciolingual and/or mesiodistal movement combined with vertical displacement
Any horizontal movement under 1 mm, felt between two instrument handles
Movement only in the mesiodistal direction, with no faciolingual movement at all
Movement that is visible only on a radiograph, as a widened PDL space with no clinical mobility

With a finger on the root while the patient occludes
With the probe tip pressed against the crown
From the width of the PDL space on a radiograph

stem: What is full-mouth debridement (D4355) for?

Definitive periodontal treatment completed in one visit, replacing scaling and root planing for patients with heavy calculus
Maintenance for a previously treated periodontitis patient who has missed their recall visits
Polishing and stain removal after SRP, billed once the root planing visits are complete

stem: When is scaling in the presence of gingival inflammation (D4346) indicated?
choices: Swollen, inflamed gingiva, generalized suprabony pockets and moderate-to-severe BOP, with no periodontitis
Active periodontitis with attachment loss, radiographic bone loss and bleeding pockets around several teeth
A healthy patient due for a routine 6-month cleaning with little or no calculus present
Implant maintenance only, for cleaning around implant abutments rather than natural teeth
ex: D4346 is for a patient never diagnosed with periodontitis, with no bone loss from it, but generalized moderate or severe gingival inflammation: swollen, inflamed gingiva, generalized suprabony pockets and moderate-to-severe BOP. It sits between a prophy and SRP and isn't reported with a prophylaxis, SRP or debridement.

stem: Which definition matches root planing?
choices: Removing rough, calculus-impregnated or contaminated cementum or surface dentin from the root
Removal of supragingival stain and plaque from enamel surfaces, finished with a rubber cup and paste
Polishing the enamel and exposed root with pumice so plaque has less to hold on to afterwards
Removing the inflamed soft-tissue lining of the pocket so a new connective-tissue attachment can form
ex: Root planing removes cementum or surface dentin that is rough, impregnated with calculus, or contaminated with toxins or microorganisms, leaving a smooth root with no ridges, roughness or catch (AAP Glossary, 2001). It stays subgingival, on root surfaces only. Polishing with a cup and paste is a different procedure.
why: Root planing is the definitive removal of rough, calculus-impregnated or contaminated cementum or surface dentin.
Removing supragingival stain and plaque with a rubber cup is coronal polishing.
Polishing enamel and root with pumice is polishing, not root planing.
That describes gingival curettage, a soft-tissue procedure on the pocket wall; root planing works on the root surface.

stem: How does instrumentation in one session compare with multiple sessions?
choices: No considerable advantage to multiple sessions
Multiple sessions double the attachment gain
Multiple sessions remove all residual calculus

why: Root debridement is inadequate about 65% of the time in pockets 5 mm or deeper (Greenstein 2000).

cue: Most of the PD drop is the swelling going down (and the recession it leaves); reattachment at the base adds the rest. No new bone.
