A rubber cup at 90° with light, intermittent pressure describes polishing.
A short, powerful pull stroke with the lower third of a sickle's blade, under the ledge of calculus, is a working scaling stroke, not exploration.

stem: Match each intraoral finger rest to where it sits.
pairs: Tooth surfaces right next to the working area
The other side of the same arch
Index finger or thumb of the non-working hand
ex: Conventional rests sit right beside the working area; cross-arch on the other side of the same arch; opposite-arch on the other jaw; finger-on-finger on the non-working hand.

likely.t: Instrumentation: finger rests, scaling vs root planing, what the ultrasonic can't do

cue: Magnetostrictive = "Metal stacks, Moves in a loop, every side works". Piezo = "Pushes in a line, sides work".
stem: Match each ultrasonic feature to what it is.
pairs: Nickel-iron metal stacks in the insert
Elliptical to orbital, so every tip surface works
Linear, so mainly the lateral surfaces work
ex: A magnetostrictive unit sends electrical energy to nickel-iron metal stacks in the insert, which vibrate in an elliptical-to-orbital pattern (about 18,000-42,000 cycles per second), so every surface of the tip can debride. A piezoelectric unit, the clinic's kind, uses crystals in the handpiece, and the tip moves linearly, so mainly its lateral surfaces work.

stem: Which areas are most commonly missed during scaling and root planing?
choices: The CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles, and distal surfaces of posterior teeth
Facial surfaces of the anterior teeth, where the gingiva is thinnest and the roots most visible
Occlusal surfaces of the molars, where calculus forms fastest
Palatal surfaces of the maxillary incisors, and nowhere else in the mouth
ex: The CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles and distal surfaces of posterior teeth are the spots most often missed: hard to see, hard to reach and easy to under-instrument.
why: The CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles and posterior distals are hard to see and reach, so they're most often missed.
Anterior facials are easy to see and reach, so they are not the commonly missed areas.
Occlusal surfaces are not where SRP is done; root surfaces are.
Maxillary incisor palatals are not the classic missed sites; distals, line angles, furcations and the CEJ are.

cue: UNC-15 = University of North Carolina, 15 mm: the periodontal probe.
stem: What is a UNC-15?
choices: A universal curette for root surfaces
ex: The UNC-15 is a periodontal probe 15 mm long, used on all teeth for probing depth, CAL and pocket form. The curved Nabers probe is for furcations, and the ODU 11/12 explorer checks root roughness.
why: The UNC-15 is the periodontal probe, 15 mm long: the exam instrument for probing depth and CAL on every tooth.
A curved furcation probe is the Nabers probe, with light and dark bands 3 mm apart.
Root roughness is checked with an explorer such as the ODU 11/12.
The universal curette is the Columbia 13/14, with two cutting edges; the UNC-15 is a probe.

cue: "4 µm in 30 s": half a minute of pumice can take the fluoride-rich top layer of enamel.
stem: How much enamel can 30 seconds of polishing with pumice paste remove?
ex: Thirty seconds of polishing with pumice can remove up to 4 µm of enamel: micrometers, so 0.004 mm, not 0.4 mm. That outermost layer holds the highest fluoride concentration, which is part of the case against routine polishing.
why: 30 seconds with pumice can remove up to 4 µm of enamel, the fluoride-rich outer layer.
40 µm is ten times the cited figure of 4 µm.
0.4 mm (400 µm) is a hundred times the cited figure.
Pumice is abrasive; it does remove enamel, up to 4 µm in 30 seconds.

stem: Which polishing technique limits enamel and tissue loss?
choices: Low-abrasion paste, slow-speed handpiece, minimal heat, cup at 90° with intermittent light pressure
Coarse paste at high speed with steady, heavy pressure so stain comes off in one pass
Pumice for a full 2 minutes per tooth, with the cup held flat and pressed firmly against the surface
Subgingival polishing down to the base of the pocket with a pointed rubber cup
ex: Polish with a low-abrasion paste on a slow-speed handpiece, keep heat down, and hold the cup at 90° with light, intermittent pressure to limit enamel and tissue loss.
why: Low-abrasion paste, slow speed, minimal heat, cup at 90° with light, intermittent pressure limits enamel and tissue loss.
Coarse paste, high speed and heavy pressure remove more enamel and build heat, the opposite of what's taught.
Two minutes of pumice per tooth with heavy pressure can strip the sulcular epithelium and remove enamel.
Polishing is not done subgingivally to the pocket base; it is selective and coronal.

cue: Polish for looks and prep: stain off before sealants or fluoride. It treats nothing below the gum.
stem: Which is a valid reason FOR polishing?
choices: Removing extrinsic stain before sealants or fluoride, and patient satisfaction
Removing subgingival calculus that the curette left behind on the root
Reducing probing depth by smoothing the soft-tissue side of the pocket wall
Removing endotoxin that is bound to the cementum of the root surface
ex: Polishing removes extrinsic stain, preps teeth for sealants or fluoride, and patients like it. It does nothing for subgingival calculus, pocket depth or endotoxin.
why: Removing extrinsic stain before sealants or fluoride, and patient satisfaction, are the valid reasons for polishing.
Polishing can't remove subgingival calculus; that takes curettes or ultrasonics.
Polishing does nothing to the soft-tissue pocket wall or probing depth.
Polishing doesn't address root-bound endotoxin; root instrumentation does.

stem: During Phase I, how do you check whether you scaled and root planed well?
choices: Explore the root surface during the session, then judge tissue response (less erythema, edema and BOP) at re-evaluation
Take a radiograph the same day and compare the calculus visible interproximally with the pre-op film to confirm that it is gone
Measure new bone fill at one week, since good root planing produces radiographic bone gain by then
Ask whether the patient reports sensitivity afterwards, since smooth, clean roots are always sensitive
ex: Check your work twice: explore the root surface during the session for any catch or roughness, then judge the tissue response at the Phase I evaluation (less erythema, edema and BOP). The patient's own hygiene weighs heavily on that result. A same-day radiograph or the patient's sensitivity doesn't measure it.
why: Explore the root during the session, then judge tissue response (less erythema, edema and BOP) at re-evaluation.
Radiographs are poor at showing small calculus deposits and don't confirm clean roots the same day.
SRP does not produce radiographic bone fill, let alone at one week.
Sensitivity is a possible side effect, not a measure of how well you root planed.

cue: No bone loss, no periodontitis: periodontitis can only live on a reduced periodontium.
stem: Which diagnosis is impossible by definition?
ex: Bone loss is what separates periodontitis from health and gingivitis, so periodontitis always sits on a reduced periodontium. Health and gingivitis can each be on an intact or a reduced periodontium.
why: Periodontitis always involves bone loss, so it can never sit on an intact periodontium.
Gingivitis on a reduced periodontium is a real diagnosis, as in the post-ortho extraction case.
Health on a reduced periodontium is a real diagnosis, such as a stable treated patient.
Gingivitis on an intact periodontium is the ordinary gingivitis diagnosis.

stem: You run the probe about 1 mm into each sulcus and score 1 where plaque comes out and 0 where it doesn't. What does this record?
choices: Presence or absence of plaque only
The amount of plaque at each site
Plaque thickness in the gingival third
ex: Running the probe about 1 mm into the sulcus and scoring 1 or 0 records only whether plaque is there, not how much; disclosing tablets are the same. Quantifying it (gingival third, half the tooth, the whole tooth) at every site would take far more chair time. It isn't a probing-depth reading.
why: This method scores 1 or 0 at each site, so it records only presence or absence of plaque.
Scoring 1 or 0 doesn't quantify plaque; measuring amount at every site would take too much chair time.
Plaque thickness in the gingival third is a quantified index, which this method doesn't give.
Probing depth is measured to the pocket base, not by sweeping 1 mm into the sulcus.

stem: You finish probing the upper right and move to the upper left. Looking back, a few upper-right sites that didn't bleed at first are now bleeding. How are they scored?
choices: As not bleeding (0), because bleeding must be immediate
Re-probe them at the next visit
ex: Delayed bleeding still counts as BOP. When you've moved on to the next quadrant or the next two teeth, look back: sites that have started bleeding since are scored 1, like any site that bleeds (BOP, like plaque, is scored 1 or 0).
why: Delayed bleeding still counts as BOP, so those sites are scored 1.
Bleeding doesn't have to be immediate; delayed bleeding counts.
Waiting for the next visit is unnecessary; delayed bleeding is recorded now as BOP.
Suppuration is pus, a separate finding; these sites are bleeding.

stem: A heavy smoker has periodontitis. Compared with a non-smoker, how will the gingiva tend to look?
choices: Less inflamed, more cyanotic, because nicotine vasoconstriction masks inflammation
More edematous and hemorrhagic, because nicotine increases blood flow to the gingival tissues
Bulbous interdental overgrowth, similar to the enlargement seen with calcium channel blockers
Exactly the same, since smoking changes bone levels but has no visible effect on the gingiva
ex: Nicotine's vasoconstriction masks inflammation, so a smoker's periodontitis tends to look cyanotic rather than edematous and hemorrhagic. Diabetes does the opposite and exaggerates it.
why: Nicotine's vasoconstriction masks inflammation, so smokers' gingiva looks paler and more cyanotic.
Nicotine reduces blood flow, so tissue looks less edematous and hemorrhagic, not more.
Bulbous interdental overgrowth is drug-induced (calcium channel blockers), not a smoking look.
Smoking does change how gingiva looks: it masks the signs of inflammation.

stem: A hypertensive patient has bulbous gingival enlargement, mostly interdental and more on the buccal/labial than the lingual/palatal. Which medication fits?
ex: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker, a classic cause of drug-induced gingival overgrowth.
why: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker, a classic cause of drug-induced gingival overgrowth.
Metformin, a diabetes drug, is not associated with gingival overgrowth.
Atorvastatin, a statin, is not a cause of gingival overgrowth.
Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor; the overgrowth classic among antihypertensives is calcium channel blockers.

stem: A site probes 5 mm and the gingival margin sits 3 mm coronal to the CEJ (recession −3 mm). What is the CAL?
ex: CAL = PD + GR = 5 + (−3) = 2 mm. Skipping the recession would record CAL 5 mm and push the case toward Stage 3 or 4.
why: CAL = PD + GR = 5 + (−3) = 2 mm.
5 mm is just the probing depth; it ignores the negative recession and over-diagnoses.
8 mm adds 3 as if it were positive recession; the margin is coronal to the CEJ, so it's −3.
3 mm is just the recession value, not the attachment level.

likely.t: CAL = PD + recession, with its sign: negative recession in Salud

cue: In health the gum sits above the CEJ, so recession is negative and PD ≠ CAL.
stem: In periodontal health on an intact periodontium, how do probing depth and CAL compare?
choices: They are not equal, because the gingival margin sits coronal to the CEJ
They are always equal, since in health the CEJ and the gingival margin sit at the same level
CAL is always larger than PD, because some attachment is lost normally with age
CAL can't be measured in health, because the CEJ is covered and can't be found
ex: In intact health the gingival margin sits slightly coronal to the CEJ and hides it, so recession is negative and CAL (PD + GR, with its sign) comes out smaller than PD. Treating PD as CAL over-diagnoses.
why: In health the margin sits coronal to the CEJ, so recession is negative and PD does not equal CAL.
In health the gingival margin is coronal to the CEJ, not level with it, so they're not equal.
Attachment loss is not a normal part of health; CAL is smaller than PD in health.
CAL can be measured in health by feeling for the CEJ with the probe.

likely.t: CAL = PD + recession, with its sign: negative recession in Salud

stem: In Salud, what happens if you leave recession blank, or type 0 without checking, at a site where the gingival margin sits coronal to the CEJ?
choices: Salud sets CAL equal to PD, over-diagnosing disease
Salud estimates the recession from the radiograph
Salud flags the site and won't save the chart
Salud records CAL as zero at that site
ex: Salud adds whatever recession you enter to PD. A blank or a 0 makes CAL equal PD: a PD 5, GR −3 site reads CAL 5 instead of 2, which can push the case toward a false Stage 3 or 4. Enter the signed value (+ or −) and Salud calculates CAL correctly.
why: A blank or a reflexive 0 makes Salud set CAL = PD, so the site reads as more attachment loss than it has.
Salud has no link to the radiograph; it uses what you enter.
Salud doesn't refuse to save; it quietly records CAL as PD.
Salud doesn't record CAL as zero; it treats recession as zero, so CAL equals PD.

likely.t: CAL = PD + recession, with its sign: negative recession in Salud

stem: How do you measure negative recession when you can't see the CEJ?
choices: Probe to the pocket base, withdraw slowly until you feel the CEJ, and read how much probe is still under the margin
Read the bone crest off a bitewing, then subtract the probing depth from that bone-level measurement
Sweep a Nabers probe horizontally along the margin and record the first point where it catches
Record recession as zero, because a CEJ you cannot see clinically means the gingival margin still sits coronal to it on that tooth
ex: Probe to the pocket base, then draw the probe out slowly until you feel the rough CEJ. The millimeters still under the margin at that point are the negative GR, which you subtract from PD to get CAL.
why: Probe to the base, withdraw slowly until you feel the CEJ, and read how much probe stays under the margin.
A bitewing shows the bone crest, not the CEJ-to-margin distance clinically, so it can't give recession.
A Nabers probe is a furcation instrument, not a way to find the CEJ under the margin.
A hidden CEJ means negative recession, not zero; recording 0 makes CAL equal PD and over-diagnoses.

likely.t: CAL = PD + recession, with its sign: negative recession in Salud

cue: Altered passive eruption is the "born that way" cover over the CEJ: physiologic, unlike inflammation or overgrowth.
stem: Which of these makes it harder to feel the CEJ for a negative recession reading, but is physiologic rather than pathologic?
ex: Altered passive eruption is physiologic: as a tooth comes in, the gingiva should migrate apically and settle at the CEJ, and in altered passive eruption it never makes that move, so the margin stays well coronal to the CEJ and hides it. Heavy inflammation and gingival overgrowth also hide the CEJ but are pathologic, and calculus or restorative margins can feel like a CEJ.
why: Altered passive eruption leaves the margin coronal to the CEJ, but it is physiologic, not disease.
Drug-induced overgrowth hides the CEJ too, but it is pathologic.
Inflammation hides the CEJ too, but it is pathologic.
Calculus can feel like a CEJ, but it is a pathologic deposit, not a physiologic variant.

stem: What is the only indication for full-mouth debridement?
choices: Calculus so heavy you can't see or explore the gingival margin to chart
Moderate periodontitis that you want to treat fully in a single visit
Heavy stain and plaque on a maintenance patient before polishing
Any subgingival calculus found during a routine adult prophylaxis visit
ex: Debridement has one indication: calculus hiding the gingival margin so completely that you can't see or explore it, so no numbers can be captured. It is not therapeutic and is never combined with SRP; the full periodontal exam follows at a later visit.
why: Debridement's only indication is calculus hiding the gingival margin so completely that you can't see or explore it, so no numbers can be captured.
Debridement is not therapeutic and never replaces or combines with SRP for periodontitis.
Stain and plaque on a maintenance patient are handled at the maintenance visit; debridement is only for margins you can't chart.
Shallow subgingival calculus is removed as part of a prophylaxis; it calls for debridement only if it hides the margin.

likely.t: Debridement has one indication and is never combined with SRP

stem: Which statement about the debridement code is correct?
choices: Half-mouth debridement can be billed with SRP
It is billed together with the periodontal exam
ex: There is only a full-mouth debridement code (D4355): no quadrant, half-mouth, lower-anterior or maxillary-posterior version exists, because it is meant for generalized calculus heavy enough to cover even chewing surfaces. Debridement is never combined with SRP, and insurance won't pay for it and a periodontal exam at the same visit, so the patient usually returns in about two weeks. At school the first perio charting is free, so the two can be combined if the tissue allows and faculty agree.
why: Debridement is billed only as a full-mouth code (D4355).
There are no quadrant codes for debridement; quadrant codes exist for SRP.
Debridement is never billed with SRP.
Insurance won't pay for debridement and a periodontal exam at the same visit.

likely.t: Debridement has one indication and is never combined with SRP

stem: Match each Glickman furcation class to its description.
pairs: Incipient: the probe just feels a catch
Cul-de-sac: bone remains on the other side
Through-and-through and clinically visible (soft tissue lost)
ex: Glickman grades by how far the probe goes: Class I is only a catch, Class II goes in but meets bone (cul-de-sac), Class III goes through, and Class IV goes through with the opening visible because the soft tissue has receded.

likely.t: Glickman furcation classes; Class II is the most regenerable

cue: Class II is the "cup": deep enough to hold a graft, with a wall still on the far side. Class III is a tunnel, nothing to hold it.
stem: Which furcation class is most amenable to regeneration?
ex: Class II (cul-de-sac) is the most amenable to regeneration: it has depth and containability, because a bony wall remains on the other side. Class I usually needs no treatment; Class III, through-and-through, has no containability and is the hardest to treat.
why: Class II has depth and a bony wall on the far side, so it can contain a graft.
Class I is just a catch at the entrance and usually needs no regeneration.
Class III is through-and-through, with no wall to contain a graft.
Class IV is through-and-through and visible, with no containability.

likely.t: Glickman furcation classes; Class II is the most regenerable

stem: Why must a Class IV furcation be watched closely at every maintenance visit?
choices: Exposed root surfaces risk root caries, and caries in the furcation makes the tooth hopeless
It always converts back to Class II once the tissue heals, so the class must be updated each visit
It is the furcation class most amenable to regeneration, so it is monitored for the right time to graft
It can't be cleaned with any aid, so it needs professional debridement at every single visit
ex: A Class IV is a Class III that has also lost the soft tissue over it, through recession or surgically, so the through-and-through furcation is visible. The patient can clean it with interdental aids or a water flosser, but the exposed root trunk risks sensitivity and root caries, and caries in a furcation makes the tooth hopeless, so keep these teeth under close watch at every maintenance visit. Class II, not IV, is the class most amenable to regeneration.
why: Exposed root surfaces in a Class IV risk root caries, and caries in the furcation makes the tooth hopeless.
Furcation classes don't revert from IV to II on healing.
Class II is the class most amenable to regeneration; a Class IV has no containing wall.
Patients can clean a Class IV with interdental aids or a water flosser.

likely.t: Glickman furcation classes; Class II is the most regenerable

cue: Nabers bands help you see, Glickman tells you the class: a catch is Class I, not a millimeter reading.
stem: The Nabers probe has light and dark bands 3 mm apart. How is a Glickman Class I furcation defined?
choices: The probe just feels a catch at the entrance
The probe enters 3 mm or less
The probe enters and meets bone on the far side
The probe passes through between the roots
ex: Furcations are charted with the Glickman classification, a qualitative grade by how far the Nabers probe goes. The bands are 3 mm apart, but Class I means the probe just feels a catch, not '3 mm or less'.
why: Class I (incipient) is a catch: Glickman grades by how far the probe goes, not by a millimeter reading.
The bands help you see, but Glickman isn't a millimeter scale: Class I is a catch, not '3 mm or less'.
Entering and meeting a bony wall on the other side is Class II, the cul-de-sac.
Passing through between the roots is Class III, through-and-through.

likely.t: Glickman furcation classes; Class II is the most regenerable

stem: What is the rolling technique used for?
choices: Finding the mucogingival junction, to measure keratinized tissue
Finding furcation entrances by rolling the probe around the root
Spreading disclosing solution evenly with a cotton applicator
Testing mobility by rolling the tooth between two handles
ex: In the mucogingival exam you measure keratinized tissue width directly or with the rolling technique: roll the mucosa coronally until you reach the mucogingival junction, beyond which it won't roll. It matters around implants as well as teeth.
why: Roll the mucosa coronally until it stops at the mucogingival junction; that gives the width of keratinized tissue.
Furcation entrances are found with the Nabers probe, not by rolling.
Disclosing solution comes from a chewed tablet and a brief rinse; it isn't part of the mucogingival exam.
Mobility is tested between two rigid instruments, not by rolling the tooth.

stem: What is fremitus?
choices: Mobility in function, felt with a finger on the tooth as the patient bites
Static mobility, tested between two rigid instrument handles
Widening of the PDL space, seen on a periapical radiograph
Vertical displacement: the tooth can be depressed into its socket on pressure
ex: Fremitus is mobility in function: rest a finger on the root while the patient brings the teeth together and feel for vibration. It can be vertical and/or horizontal and is palpated, not seen, unless extreme. Static mobility is tested with two rigid instruments, and a depressible tooth is ready for extraction.
why: Fremitus is mobility in function: a finger rests on the root while the patient brings the teeth together, feeling for vibration.
Static mobility between two rigid instruments is the Miller mobility test, not fremitus.
A widened PDL space is a radiographic finding, not fremitus, which is palpated.
A tooth depressible in its socket is Miller Class 3 mobility, ready for extraction, not fremitus.

likely.t: Fremitus is palpated; Miller mobility classes

stem: Maxillary premolars are fremitus-positive in a patient missing posterior teeth. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Lack of posterior support, so the premolars are doing the work of molars
Drug-induced gingival overgrowth, pushing the premolars out of their normal occlusal contacts
Altered passive eruption, leaving short clinical crowns that take up the excess occlusal load
Root caries on the premolars, weakening the roots so that normal chewing forces cause fremitus
ex: Lack of posterior support makes the premolars do the work of molars: occlusal trauma on a reduced periodontium, felt as fremitus. Parafunction and overjet/overbite can do the same. Positive fremitus means finding out why the tooth carries that load.
why: With no posterior support, the premolars carry molar loads, causing occlusal trauma and fremitus.
Gingival overgrowth doesn't cause fremitus; it changes tissue, not occlusal load.
Altered passive eruption affects tissue position, not the occlusal forces that cause fremitus.
Root caries isn't the cause; loss of posterior support overloads the premolars.

likely.t: Fremitus is palpated; Miller mobility classes

stem: Where do you record occlusal findings such as wear patterns, erosion and parafunction?
choices: In the notes section, since the perio chart has no field for them
In the mobility row, next to the Miller class for each tooth
In the furcation column, beside the Glickman class for molars
They aren't recorded anywhere in the perio exam, only in the restorative chart
ex: The perio chart has no place for occlusal findings, so wear patterns, erosion, vertical defects and parafunctional habits go in the notes section. They matter because mobility isn't always from periodontitis alone: it can be occlusal trauma on a reduced periodontium, and treating a 5 mm pocket won't resolve grade 2 mobility unless the occlusion is addressed.
why: The perio chart has no field for wear, erosion or parafunction, so they go in the notes.
The mobility row holds Miller classes only.
The furcation column holds furcation classes only.
Occlusal findings are recorded in the perio exam's notes because they affect perio treatment.

likely.t: Mobility from occlusion: treating the pocket won't fix it

cue: "X-rays out, chart away": the films show the calculus and root anatomy, the instrument finds the pocket base.
stem: When you sit down for SRP, what should you have open in front of you?
choices: The radiographs, rather than the probing chart
The probing chart, to target the deepest pockets
ex: Open the radiographs, not the chart (Dr. Kaur's tip; screenshot them, since Salud times out). The instrument will find the pocket and its base is your limit, while the x-rays tell you where the calculus, PA lesions and root anatomy are.
why: Open the radiographs: they show the calculus, PA lesions and root anatomy you'll meet.
The instrument finds the pocket, and its base is your limit, so there's no need to hunt the chart for deep pockets.
The medical history matters, but it doesn't guide the instrument the way the radiographs do.
Working by feel alone ignores the radiographic map of calculus and root anatomy.

likely.t: Look at the radiographs first: what they show before you probe

cue: "Bugs light the match (25%), the host burns the house (75%)".
stem: Roughly what share of periodontal destruction is caused by the host response rather than the bacteria?
ex: Bacteria (bringing endotoxin/LPS) account for about 25%. The host's inflammatory mediators and osteoclasts account for about 75%, yet SRP targets the bacteria, which calms the host response.
why: About 75% of the destruction comes from the host's inflammatory mediators and osteoclasts.
About 25% is the bacterial share, not the host's.
50% splits it evenly; the class figure is about 75% host, 25% bacteria.
Bacteria contribute about 25%, so the host isn't responsible for nearly all of it.

likely.t: The host does 75% of the damage, bacteria 25%

stem: In the host-bacteria model of periodontitis, what initiates the disease and what drives its progression?
choices: Plaque bacteria initiate it; the host response drives it
The host response initiates it; plaque bacteria drive it
Calculus initiates it; smoking drives its progression
Genetics initiates it; plaque bacteria drive it
ex: Plaque bacteria initiate periodontitis; the host's immune response drives its progression, doing about 75% of the damage through inflammatory mediators and osteoclasts. SRP targets the bacteria, and removing them calms the host. Dr. Kaur flagged this diagram in class: "That's going to be on the quiz."
why: Plaque bacteria initiate periodontitis; the host immune response drives its progression.
That reverses the model: bacteria initiate, the host response drives progression.
Calculus is a plaque-retentive irritant and smoking a risk factor; neither is the initiator or the driver in this model.
Genetics adds risk; plaque bacteria initiate and the host response drives progression.

likely.t: The host does 75% of the damage, bacteria 25%

cue: "1 week, 1 month, 1 season": JE ~7-10 days, connective tissue 4-6 weeks (that's when you re-evaluate), collagen matures over 3-6 months. Calculus left at that visit: remove it, evaluate again in 2 weeks.
stem: Match each event after SRP to its timing, as taught in class.
pairs: A second Phase I evaluation, after calculus left at the first one is removed
ex: The junctional epithelium reattaches first (7-10 days), connective tissue by 4-6 weeks (which is why the Phase I evaluation is then: 4-6 weeks, not months), and collagen fibers keep maturing and orienting for 3-6 months. The 2 weeks is only for a second evaluation: if the probe finds residual calculus at the first one, remove it and do another Phase I evaluation 2 weeks later.

likely.t: What SRP aims for, and the Phase I evaluation at 4-6 weeks: what to expect, how it heals

cue: The pocket stops shrinking by 4-6 weeks, so re-evaluate then: waiting 3 months just delays plan B.
stem: Why not wait 3 months to re-evaluate after SRP?
choices: The maximum PD reduction is seen by 4-6 weeks; waiting longer gives no additional reduction
Collagen can't mature before 3 months, so probing any earlier tears the new attachment
Insurance requires re-evaluation at 4-6 weeks, even though healing continues for months after
Calculus reforms after about 6 weeks, so the pockets would look deeper again if you waited
ex: By 4–6 weeks the maximum PD reduction has happened. Waiting longer adds no further reduction, it only delays deciding what the non-responding sites need.
why: Maximum PD reduction is reached by 4-6 weeks; waiting 3 months adds nothing and delays decisions.
Probing at 4-6 weeks doesn't tear the new attachment; re-evaluation is routinely done then.
The reason is biologic (maximum reduction by 4-6 weeks), not an insurance rule.
Calculus reforming isn't the stated reason; the PD reduction has simply plateaued by 4-6 weeks.

likely.t: What SRP aims for, and the Phase I evaluation at 4-6 weeks: what to expect, how it heals

stem: Is scaling a supragingival or a subgingival procedure?
choices: Supragingival only; root planing does the subgingival part
Supragingival, except in pockets deeper than 3 mm
ex: Scaling removes soft and hard deposits from tooth and root surfaces, and from fixed or removable prostheses, both supra- and subgingivally. Root planing stays subgingival, on root surfaces only. Clinically the two are done together.
why: Scaling removes deposits from tooth and root surfaces both above and below the gingival margin.
Scaling isn't limited to above the margin; it works supra- and subgingivally, and root planing is done together with it.
Subgingival only, on root surfaces, describes root planing, not scaling.
No pocket depth makes scaling supragingival only; it works on tooth and root surfaces above and below the margin.

likely.t: Instrumentation: finger rests, scaling vs root planing, what the ultrasonic can't do

cue: Never had perio = prophylaxis, even with some subgingival calculus. Maintenance is only for patients already treated for periodontitis.
stem: A patient who has never had periodontitis has 1-2 mm of subgingival calculus in normal sulci. What is the appropriate procedure?
ex: Subgingival calculus doesn't make it periodontitis, and prophylaxis is preventive. Maintenance is supportive therapy only for patients already treated for periodontitis.
why: A never-periodontitis patient with normal sulci gets a prophylaxis, even with some subgingival calculus.
Periodontal maintenance is only for patients already treated for periodontitis.
SRP treats periodontitis; subgingival calculus alone doesn't make it periodontitis.

cue: SRP is a root-surface job: anything that lives off the root (bacteria in the soft-tissue wall) or blocks the blade (grooves, furcations, margins, blind access) is a limitation.
stem: Which are limitations of scaling and root planing? Select all that apply.
choices: It is a blinded, tactile procedure
Motile bacteria invade the pocket lining
Calculus is always left behind in pockets of 5 mm or more
Ultrasonic tips can't be used below the gingival margin
ex: Blind, tactile access, motile bacteria in the soft-tissue lining, restorative margins and over-removed cementum are all on the taught list. Deep pockets are harder, not hopeless: a 5 mm pocket doesn't mean calculus is left every time. Ultrasonics work subgingivally; they just can't root plane. Also on the list: furcations, grooves and concavities, patient compliance with hygiene, and operator skill.
why: Belongs: SRP is a blinded procedure; tactile sensation and proprioception are your guide in the pocket.
Belongs: motile bacteria invade the soft-tissue pocket lining, while SRP only targets the pocket itself.
Belongs: overhanging, subgingival, open or rough margins both collect plaque and resist cleaning.
Belongs: chasing a smooth root can remove too much cementum, causing hypersensitivity.
Doesn't belong: deeper pockets are harder to reach, but a 5 mm pocket doesn't mean calculus is left every time.
Doesn't belong: the clinic's piezoelectric ultrasonic can be used subgingivally; what it can't do is root plane.

stem: Which can a radiograph tell you before you probe? Select all that apply.
choices: Whether bone loss is localized or generalized
ex: Before any clinical data, a radiograph shows whether there is bone loss, where it is (localized or generalized) and its pattern (horizontal, vertical or both), plus tipped teeth, fused roots, root proximity, calculus, sinus proximity and periapical lesions. BOP and keratinized tissue are clinical findings. Keep the x-rays open during SRP, not the chart.
why: Belongs: a radiograph shows whether bone loss is localized or generalized.
Belongs: a radiograph shows the pattern of bone loss: horizontal, vertical or both.
Belongs: root proximity and fused roots show on the film, and root proximity matters for surgical and non-surgical therapy.
Belongs: calculus and a periapical lesion both show on the film, so you know what you'll meet before you touch the patient.
Doesn't belong: bleeding on probing is a clinical finding that only probing can show.
Doesn't belong: keratinized tissue width is measured clinically, directly or with the rolling technique.

likely.t: Look at the radiographs first: what they show before you probe

stem: On a maxillary first molar, about how far from the CEJ is the distal (distopalatal) furcation entrance?
ex: As taught (Bower 1979), the maxillary first molar's entrances sit about 3.6 mm (mesiopalatal), 4.2 mm (buccal) and 4.8 mm (distopalatal) from the CEJ; the exam-review guide rounds them to 3, 3.5 and 5 mm. Either way the distal one is the most apical. About 8 mm is the maxillary premolar's.
why: The distal (distopalatal) entrance is the most apical: about 5 mm in the exam-review guide (4.8 mm as taught).
About 3 mm is the guide's figure for the mesial entrance, the one closest to the CEJ.
About 3.5 mm is the guide's figure for the buccal entrance.
About 8 mm is the maxillary premolar's furcation depth, not the molar's.

stem: Which molar has a shorter root trunk — the first or the second maxillary molar?
ex: The first molar has the shorter root trunk, so its furcation starts closer to the CEJ and is exposed by less attachment loss.
why: The first molar has the shorter root trunk, so less attachment loss is needed to reach its furcation.

stem: Roughly what percentage of maxillary premolars have two root cones?

why: About 40% of maxillary premolars have two root cones, so they can have a furcation.
About 10% is too low; about 40% of maxillary premolars have two roots.
About 75% is too high; about 40% of maxillary premolars have two roots.
About 5% is too low; about 40% of maxillary premolars have two roots.

cue: Class I = "just the doorway": smooth the entrance (furcation plasty) and root plane. No surgery for a catch.
stem: Furcation Class I is best managed with which treatment?
ex: A Class I furcation is only incipient, so SRP plus furcation plasty (smoothing the entrance so it can be cleaned) is enough.

stem: The exam-review guide lists GTR as a Class II furcation option for which teeth?
ex: The guide lists GTR for Class II mandibular molars. The lecture adds the buccal furcation of maxillary molars as an equally good candidate; their mesial and distal (interproximal) degree II furcations are much less suited because access is limited.

stem: Which bone architecture pattern has interdental bone sitting apical to its midfacial and midlingual margins?
ex: In reverse (negative) architecture, the interdental bone sits lower (apical) than the facial and lingual bone, producing craters.

In positive architecture, the healthy pattern, interdental bone sits coronal to the facial and lingual bone.
In flat architecture the interdental and radicular bone are at about the same level.

stem: In positive bone architecture, where does the interdental bone sit relative to the midfacial/midlingual bone?

stem: Why does osseous surgery reshape the bone to follow the gingiva?
choices: Gingiva regains its scallop, so pockets recur if bone doesn't match
Bone always grows back to its original level within a year
The gingiva takes whatever shape the bone underneath is given
Flat bone keeps the teeth from becoming more mobile after surgery

stem: When is the Phase I re-evaluation done?

The same day as the last root planing

stem: At re-evaluation, a patient's hygiene is good but 6-7 mm pockets remain. What is the next step?

Osseous surgery to eliminate the remaining pockets

Creating an environment the patient can keep clean

Insurance requires at least two cleanings before any surgery
Phase I alone always eliminates the need for surgery

stem: According to the 1981 study on root planing, what happens in pockets deeper than 5 mm?

Calculus removal is as complete as in shallow pockets
Failure becomes possible but is uncommon

stem: What is the difference between ostectomy and osteoplasty?

Ostectomy reshapes bone; osteoplasty removes the whole alveolar process

Flattening the interproximal bone is step 3.

A concavity that holds the gingiva in place

Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true

stem: Which are contraindications to resective periodontal surgery? Select all that apply.

Belongs: uncontrolled systemic disease is a contraindication.

Belongs: SRP is the core of Phase I.

The CEJ and the root apex

stem: Which teeth are most likely to develop furcation involvement after only minimal attachment loss?
choices: Multi-rooted teeth with short root trunks
Multi-rooted teeth with long root trunks
ex: With a 2 mm root trunk, 2 mm of attachment loss reaches the furcation. Long trunks delay involvement, and divergent roots make treatment easier, not involvement likelier.
why: With a short trunk (say 2 mm), only 2 mm of attachment loss reaches the furcation.
A long trunk takes more attachment loss before the furcation is involved.
Single-rooted teeth have no furcation to involve.
Widely divergent roots make treatment easier; they don't make involvement come sooner.

cue: Upper first molar entrances count up going around: mesial ~3.6, buccal ~4.2, distal ~4.8. Lowers are shallow: ~2.4-2.5.
stem: From the CEJ, the furcation entrances of a maxillary first molar sit, from closest to farthest:
choices: All three at the same depth
ex: As taught (Bower 1979): mesiopalatal about 3.6 mm, buccal about 4.2 mm, distopalatal about 4.8 mm. The buccal is the narrowest entrance, not the closest one.
why: As taught (Bower): mesiopalatal about 3.6 mm, buccal about 4.2 mm, distopalatal about 4.8 mm.

likely.t: Bower's furcation entrance depths: which is closest to the CEJ

stem: How far from the CEJ are the furcation entrances of a mandibular first molar, as taught?
choices: About 2.4-2.5 mm, shallower than the maxillary molar's
About 4-5 mm, a little deeper than the maxillary molar's
About 8 mm, like a maxillary premolar
About 3.6 mm buccal and 4.8 mm lingual

stem: Why is the lingual furcation of a mandibular molar usually a little more apical than the buccal?
choices: The lingual root is always longer
The intermediate bifurcation ridge sits on the buccal
ex: Mandibular molars have a lingual angulation, which pushes the lingual furcation slightly apically. The hourglass shape belongs to the mesial root and affects cleaning, not entrance depth.

cue: Lower mesial root = "hourglass, always hollow": a 0.7 mm dip facing the furcation 100% of the time.
stem: Which root surface facing a furcation has the deepest developmental depression, present 100% of the time?
choices: The mesial root of the mandibular first molar (about 0.7 mm)
The mesiobuccal root of the maxillary first molar (about 0.3 mm)
The palatal root of the maxillary first molar (about 0.1 mm)
The distal root of the mandibular first molar (about 0.5 mm)

why: The mandibular first molar's mesial root has the deepest furcal depression, about 0.7 mm, in 100% of teeth.
The maxillary mesiobuccal root's depression is about 0.3 mm and present 94% of the time, not 100%.
The maxillary palatal root's depression is shallow (0.1 mm) and present only about 17% of the time.

stem: On the maxillary first molar, the furcal surface of which root has a developmental depression about 94% of the time?
choices: None; maxillary molar roots are convex
ex: Mesiobuccal: 0.3 mm in 94%. The distobuccal (31%) and palatal (17%) roots have shallower 0.1 mm depressions less often.

cue: The blade is bigger than the door: most entrances <1 mm, a curette face 0.75-1.10 mm.

stem: Which maxillary molar furcation is affected most often?
ex: The buccal is most commonly affected, then the mesiopalatal, then the distopalatal. Maxillary molars overall are affected more than mandibular molars, and on mandibular molars the buccal furcation is affected most.

stem: What is the primary cause of furcation involvement?
choices: Progressive attachment loss from inflammatory periodontal disease
Cervical enamel projections that funnel plaque into the furcation
Restoration overhangs that hold plaque at the furcation entrance
Short root trunks that put the furcation close to the CEJ

cue: CEP = a widow's peak of enamel pointing into the furcation, and gums can't stick to enamel, so it's a plaque slide.
stem: Why does a cervical enamel projection predispose a molar to furcation involvement?

The enamel is softer than cementum and decays into the furcation
It narrows the furcation entrance so a curette can't enter

stem: How does a cervical enamel projection form?

Cementum is laid down over the enamel at the CEJ
An ameloblast rest becomes trapped in the PDL
Root dentin resorbs and enamel grows into the defect

stem: Cervical enamel projections are most common on:

stem: On which surface is a cervical enamel projection most likely?

stem: A Grade 1 cervical enamel projection is found on #30 with no bone or attachment loss. What is the usual management?

stem: A periodontally stable patient has 2-3 mm probing depths everywhere except a lone Class II furcation on #19 buccal. What should you look for first?

A systemic cause such as diabetes

cue: Found a furcation? Don't rush in: treat the disease and the local factor, not the anatomy.

cue: Tunnel = make it a IV on purpose, so a brush fits. Price: root caries.
stem: What does a tunnel preparation deliberately create?
ex: Bone is removed so the furcation is through-and-through and exposed, letting the patient pass an interproximal brush. It's limited to mandibular molars with long, divergent roots, and caries in tunneled molars is common. A single-rooted tooth is what hemisection makes.

stem: What is the main complication of tunneled molars?

stem: Which root is removed most often in root resection?

The distal root of the mandibular first molar

stem: What separates a hemisection from a root resection?

Hemisection keeps the whole crown and removes only the root
Hemisection is done only on maxillary molars, never mandibular
ex: Root resection (amputation) removes a root at the level of the furcation and leaves the crown. Hemisection removes the root with its portion of the crown, usually on mandibular molars, making a single-rooted tooth. Both need endodontic treatment first.
why: Hemisection removes the root with its part of the crown, making a single-rooted tooth.
Keeping the whole crown and removing only the root describes root resection (amputation).
Hemisection is usually done on mandibular molars.
Both hemisection and root resection need endodontic treatment first.

stem: In the root separation/resection sequence, how far from the bone crest should the provisional restoration's margins end?
choices: At least 3 mm coronal to the crest
Exactly at the level of the bone crest
About 1 mm apical to the bone crest
ex: Margins of the provisional end at least 3 mm coronal to the bone crest, after periodontal surgery removes the bone defects around the remaining roots. The final restoration uses a rigid framework and minimizes lateral forces.
why: Provisional margins end at least 3 mm coronal to the bone crest, after surgery removes the bone defects.
A margin at the crest would invade the attachment apparatus.
Apical to the crest is inside the bone, which is never acceptable.
Leaving anything at the fornix creates a plaque trap; margins stay well coronal to the crest.

stem: Which treatment comes first in the root resection sequence?
ex: Endodontics first (with the access filled directly with amalgam or composite), then a provisional, then root separation and resection, then periodontal surgery, then the final restoration.
why: Endodontic treatment comes first, with the access filled directly with amalgam or composite.
Root separation and resection follow endodontics and the provisional.
Periodontal surgery comes after the root is separated and resected.
The final prosthesis is the last step.

stem: Approximately what percentage of maxillary premolars have two roots, and how far from the CEJ is their furcation entrance?
ex: About 40% have two roots, with a mean entrance about 8 mm from the CEJ: a long trunk and short roots. The maxillary first premolar also has a mesial developmental depression next to the furcation, present 100% of the time.
why: About 40% have two roots, with a mean furcation entrance about 8 mm from the CEJ.
About 2.5 mm is the mandibular molar's furcation depth, not the premolar's.
About 10% is too low; about 40% of maxillary premolars have two roots.
About 75% is too high and 4 mm is closer to a maxillary molar's buccal entrance.

pbox: Stable; probing depths 2-3 mm everywhere, no bone loss
PD 5 mm into the furcation; the Nabers probe engages and catches when pulled occlusally
A narrow strip of enamel runs from the buccal CEJ into the furcation
stem: What is the best next step for #30?
choices: Flap access, remove the enamel projection, and debride the furcation
Observe the projection and recheck the furcation at each recall
ex: This is a Grade 3 CEP (it enters the furcation) with attachment loss (a Glickman Grade II furcation), so removal is indicated: thin enamel comes off with a diamond or finishing bur, usually through a flap, along with debridement. Observation only fits a CEP without bone or attachment loss. Tunneling is for deep Class II-III on long, divergent roots and invites caries.
why: A Grade 3 CEP with attachment loss (Glickman Grade II) should be removed, usually through a flap, with debridement.
Observation fits only a CEP without bone or attachment loss; this one already has loss.
Extraction is far too aggressive for a correctable local cause in a stable patient.
Tunneling is for deep Class II-III furcations on long, divergent roots and invites caries.

likely.t: Furcation class from the Nabers probe, and the treatment by class

pbox: 3-unit bridge #29-#31, intact; #31 has had a root canal
Vertical fracture of the mesial root; furcation now involved
stem: The patient wants to keep his bridge. Which treatment from the lecture lets him?
choices: Resect the fractured mesial root at the furcation
Tunnel the furcation so a brush can pass through
Regenerate the furcation with a graft and membrane
Leave the root and debride the furcation at recalls
ex: Dr. Litz's example of root resection still in use: the bridge abutment #31, already root-canal treated, fractures its mesial root while the distal root is sound, so the fractured root is removed at the furcation and the bridge is kept. On its own, a vertically fractured root on a root-canal-treated molar means the tooth comes out; here the sound distal root lets only the mesial root go.
why: Dr. Litz's example: the fractured mesial root is removed at the furcation and the sound distal root keeps the bridge; the tooth already has the root canal that resection requires.
Tunneling doesn't treat a fractured root, which has to come out.
Regeneration can't fix a vertically fractured root.
Debriding doesn't stop the breakdown around a vertically fractured root; the root has to come out.

stem: Which consideration from the lecture weighs most against saving #31?
choices: It has no strategic value: it's a non-functioning tooth
Grade III furcations can always be regenerated instead
Its long root trunk makes it ideal for resection
A Grade III furcation can never be maintained
ex: Strategic value is one of the factors in deciding whether to treat: with #2 missing, #31 is non-functioning, and with a Grade III furcation and mobility, it may not be worth saving. Regeneration offers degree III furcations no advantage over conventional surgery.
why: With #2 missing, #31 is non-functioning, so its strategic value is low against a Grade III furcation and mobility.
Regeneration offers degree III furcations no advantage over conventional surgery.
Long root trunks make teeth poor resection candidates, not ideal ones.
Grade III furcations can be treated (tunnel, root resection); the lecture's reason against this tooth was that it doesn't function.

cue: Contributing factors you can FIX: CEP, enamel pearl, overhang, the ridge (odontoplasty). Root trunk length you can't.
stem: Which local factors that contribute to furcation involvement can the clinician remove or alter? Select all that apply.
ex: CEPs and small enamel pearls can be removed with a bur (odontoplasty), and overhangs corrected. Root trunk length and the molar's angulation are anatomy you can't change, though they affect risk and treatment choice.
why: Belongs: a CEP can be removed with a bur (odontoplasty).
Belongs: an overhang can be corrected or replaced.
Belongs: a small enamel pearl can be removed with a bur.
Doesn't belong: root trunk length is fixed anatomy, though it affects risk and treatment.
Doesn't belong: the molar's lingual angulation is anatomy you can't change.

stem: Which make a patient a poor candidate for furcation regeneration, as taught? Select all that apply.
choices: A root canal filling in the tooth
ex: Uncontrolled diabetes, immunocompromise, smoking, poor compliance and poor hygiene all count against regeneration. A root canal filling is not a contraindication, and a thicker biotype favors success.
why: Belongs: uncontrolled diabetes counts against regeneration.
Belongs: smoking counts against regeneration.
Belongs: poor hygiene and compliance doom regeneration; the patient must keep it clean.
Doesn't belong: a root canal filling is not a contraindication.
Doesn't belong: a thicker biotype favors success.

stem: Which statements about root resection are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: It commits the patient to endodontic and restorative treatment
It is limited to deep Class II and Class III furcations
The distobuccal root of the maxillary first molar is removed most often
It removes the root together with its part of the crown
It is the first choice for teeth with long root trunks
ex: Removing the root with its part of the crown is hemisection. Long root trunks generally make teeth poor candidates for resection.
why: Belongs: resection requires endodontics first and restoration after.
Belongs: resection is limited to deep Class II and Class III furcations.
Belongs: the maxillary first molar's distobuccal root is removed most often.
Doesn't belong: removing the root with its part of the crown is hemisection; resection leaves the crown.
Doesn't belong: long root trunks mean short roots, which make teeth poor resection candidates.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Maxillary molars are affected by furcation involvement more often than mandibular molars.
2. On maxillary molars, the distopalatal furcation is affected most often.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false: the buccal furcation is affected most, then the mesiopalatal, then the distopalatal.
why: Statement 2 is false: on maxillary molars the buccal furcation is affected most, not the distopalatal.
Statement 1 is true: maxillary molars are affected more often than mandibular molars.
Statement 1 is true, and statement 2 is false: the buccal is most affected, then mesiopalatal, then distopalatal.
Statement 1 is true, and statement 2 is false: the distopalatal is affected least, not most.

likely.t: The maxillary buccal furcation is affected most

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A furcation arrow on a radiograph should not be the sole tool for detecting furcation involvement.
2. Furcation arrows are typically seen at the buccal furcation of mandibular molars.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Statement 1 is true: many involved furcations show no arrow. Statement 2 is false: arrows mark mesiopalatal and distopalatal lesions of maxillary molars. Mandibular molar furcation bone loss is usually easy to see directly.
why: Statement 2 is false: arrows mark mesiopalatal and distopalatal furcations of maxillary molars.
Statement 1 is true: many involved furcations show no arrow, so it can't be the sole tool.
Statement 1 is true, and statement 2 is false: mandibular molar furcation bone loss is usually seen directly, without an arrow.
Statement 1 is true, not false, and statement 2 is false: arrows are a maxillary molar sign.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Tunneling is best suited to maxillary molars, whose three roots splay widely.
2. Root caries is rare in tunneled molars, since a brush can pass through.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Both are false. Tunneling surgically creates a Glickman Grade IV so an interproximal brush can pass through, and it is limited to mandibular molars with sufficiently long, divergent roots. Its problem is caries: root surfaces decay quickly, so caries in tunneled molars is common.
why: Statement 1 is false: tunneling is limited to mandibular molars; statement 2 is false too: caries in tunneled molars is common.
Tunneling is limited to mandibular molars with sufficiently long, divergent roots, and caries in tunneled molars is common.
Statement 1 is false too: tunneling is limited to mandibular molars with long, divergent roots.
Statement 2 is false too: caries in tunneled molars is common, since root surfaces decay quickly.

stem: All of the following are contributing factors for furcation involvement EXCEPT:
ex: Widely spaced roots are favorable: instruments reach in, in SRP and in surgery. Closely approximated or fused roots are the contributing factor. CEPs, overhangs and intermediate bifurcation ridges all hold plaque.
why: This is the exception: widely spaced roots are favorable, letting instruments reach in; close or fused roots contribute.
CEPs are a contributing factor: no connective-tissue attachment forms on enamel, so plaque is funneled into the furcation.
Overhangs are a contributing factor: they hold plaque near the furcation.
Intermediate bifurcation ridges are a contributing factor: they leave a plaque trap above them.

stem: All of the following are recommended for a Class II furcation EXCEPT:
ex: Class II recommendations: furcation plasty, regeneration (GTR), root resection or extraction. Observation without therapy fits early (Class I) involvement with no alterable local factor.
why: This is the exception: observation without therapy fits early Class I involvement with no alterable local factor.
Furcation plasty is a recommended Class II option.
Regeneration (GTR) is a recommended Class II option.
Root resection is a recommended option for deep Class II furcations.

stem: All of the following are true of cervical enamel projections EXCEPT:
choices: They occur more often on maxillary than mandibular molars
They are more likely on second molars than first molars
They are more likely on the buccal surface than the lingual
ex: The reverse: about 30% of mandibular molars vs about 15% of maxillary molars. The rest are true.
why: This is the false one: CEPs are more common on mandibular molars (about 30%) than maxillary (about 15%).
True: CEPs are more likely on second molars.
True: CEPs are more likely on the buccal surface.
True: a Grade 3 CEP extends into the furcation.

stem: All of the following are steps of furcation regeneration surgery as taught EXCEPT:
choices: Leaving enamel projections in place to support the graft
A sulcular incision with a full-thickness flap
Securing a barrier membrane with a resorbable sling suture
ex: Root anomalies such as enamel projections and pearls are removed, since no connective-tissue attachment forms on enamel. The flap is then secured coronally, and the patient skips mechanical plaque removal at the site for up to 4 weeks.
why: This is the exception: enamel projections and pearls are removed, since no connective-tissue attachment forms on enamel.
A step: access is through a sulcular incision with a full-thickness flap.
A step: the exposed root surfaces are cleaned before grafting.
A step: the barrier membrane is held with a resorbable sling suture.

stem: In the root resection sequence, all of the following should be avoided EXCEPT:
choices: Removing bone defects around the remaining roots
Exposing the interradicular bone during separation
Leaving parts of the furcation fornix behind
Leaving sharp angles on the remaining roots
ex: Periodontal surgery to remove bone defects around the remaining roots is part of the sequence. When separating the roots, avoid exposing the interradicular bone, leaving fornix behind, perforating the canals and leaving sharp angles.
why: This is the exception: removing bone defects around the remaining roots is part of the sequence, not avoided.
Avoided: exposing the interradicular bone when separating the roots.
Avoided: leaving parts of the fornix behind, which leaves a plaque trap.
Avoided: sharp angles on the remaining roots, which can't be cleaned and concentrate stress.

stem: Match each classification to what it grades.
pairs: Grades I-IV by how far the probe goes, up to visible through-and-through
Degrees 1-3 by millimeters of horizontal loss
Subclasses A-C by millimeters of vertical loss
Grades 1-3 by how far the enamel reaches toward the furcation
ex: Glickman (1953) and Hamp (1975) both describe horizontal destruction (Hamp in millimeters: under 3, over 3, through). Tarnow and Fletcher (1984) add the vertical component: A 0-3, B 4-6, C 7+ mm. CEPs have their own grades by how far apically they reach: 1 dips, 2 approaches, 3 enters the furcation.

stem: What depth and radiographic defect angle make an intrabony defect the best candidate for regeneration?
choices: Deeper than 3 mm, with an angle of 25° or less
Shallower than 3 mm, with an angle of 25° or less
Deeper than 3 mm, with an angle of 45° or more
Shallower than 3 mm, with an angle of 45° or more
ex: Defects deeper than 3 mm with a radiographic defect angle of 25° or less were reported most amenable to conventional GTR-based regeneration, and Nibali's 2021 review agrees: deeper, narrower defects gain more CAL and bone. A choice that gets only one of the two right is the trap; both features count.
why: Deep (over 3 mm) and narrow (25° or less): the combination reported most amenable to conventional GTR-based regeneration.
The narrow angle is right, but a shallow defect gains less; depth had the strongest evidence of any defect feature.
The depth is right, but a wide defect can't hold the clot and graft the way a narrow one does.
Shallow and wide is the poorest combination: both features predict less CAL and bone gain.

likely.t: 3-wall (most contained) defects regenerate best: more walls, a steeper angle, more depth

cue: Over 3 mm deep, 25° or less: deep and narrow.

stem: Which wall configuration is the best candidate for periodontal regeneration?
ex: A 3-wall defect has the most bony walls to hold the clot and graft and bring in cells and vessels, so it regenerates most predictably; the exam-review guide calls 3-wall defects the best candidates. The decision tree ranks 3-wall > circumferential ≥ 2-wall > 1-wall.
why: A 3-wall defect has the most bony walls to hold the clot and supply cells, so it regenerates most predictably; the exam-review guide calls it the best candidate.
Circumferential defects rank just behind 3-wall ones on the decision tree (3-wall > circumferential ≥ 2-wall > 1-wall).
A 2-wall crater has a wall fewer than a 3-wall defect, so it's less predictable.
A predominantly 1-wall defect is non-supportive anatomy, the least predictable of all.

likely.t: 3-wall (most contained) defects regenerate best: more walls, a steeper angle, more depth

stem: What are amelogenins, the active component of EMD, involved in?
choices: Enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during tooth development
Dentin and pulp formation, guiding the odontoblasts of the developing root
Alveolar bone formation, signaling the osteoblasts around an erupting tooth
Root resorption, clearing the primary roots so that the permanent teeth can erupt
ex: Amelogenins, the main enamel matrix proteins in EMD, are involved in enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during tooth development. EMD borrows that to regrow attachment; alone or with a graft, it gives outcomes similar to GTR.
why: Amelogenins, the main enamel matrix proteins, drive enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during development; EMD borrows that to regrow attachment.
Odontoblasts and dentin aren't what amelogenins direct; they are enamel matrix proteins.
Amelogenins aren't bone signals; on the deck, the agent that is chemotactic and mitogenic for bone cells is rhPDGF-BB.
Amelogenins build tissue during development; they don't resorb primary roots.

likely.t: Grafts and biologics: DFDBA exposes BMP, EMD (porcine amelogenins, consent), rhPDGF-BB with β-TCP

stem: What does rhPDGF-BB do in a regenerative graft?
choices: Chemotactic and mitogenic for bone and PDL cells, and angiogenic
A barrier that keeps the gingival epithelium off the root surface
Amelogenins that mimic attachment formation during development
An osteoconductive scaffold that stabilizes the blood clot
ex: rhPDGF-BB (recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor BB) is chemotactic and mitogenic for bone and PDL cells and angiogenic, so it drives revascularization. The β-TCP it is paired with is the scaffold that holds the clot and the space; don't confuse the signal with the matrix.
why: rhPDGF-BB is chemotactic (draws bone and PDL cells in), mitogenic (makes them multiply) and angiogenic (drives revascularization).
That's the GTR membrane, a physical barrier; rhPDGF-BB is a growth factor.
That's EMD, an extract of enamel matrix proteins, mostly amelogenins.
That's the β-TCP scaffold the exam-review guide pairs with rhPDGF-BB: the scaffold is the matrix, the growth factor the signal.

likely.t: Grafts and biologics: DFDBA exposes BMP, EMD (porcine amelogenins, consent), rhPDGF-BB with β-TCP

cue: PDGF: call cells, copy cells, grow vessels.

stem: What is the primary role of a β-TCP scaffold in a regenerative graft?
choices: Osteoconductive matrix that prevents soft-tissue collapse and stabilizes the clot
Antibiotic delivery, releasing drug slowly into the defect to suppress pocket bacteria after surgery
Replacing the need for a flap, because the scaffold can be injected through the pocket without surgery
Conditioning the root surface so that new cementum can form on it after debridement
ex: β-TCP is the scaffold: an osteoconductive matrix that keeps soft tissue from collapsing into the defect and holds the clot still.
why: β-TCP is an osteoconductive scaffold: it keeps soft tissue from collapsing into the defect and holds the clot still while bone grows in.
β-TCP carries no antibiotic. Slow local drug release is what products like Arestin or Atridox do, not a graft scaffold.
A regenerative graft still needs a flap for access and debridement; β-TCP is packed into an opened defect, not injected through the pocket.
β-TCP does not condition the root. Root conditioning uses separate agents (such as EDTA); the scaffold's job is space and clot stability.

likely.t: Grafts and biologics: DFDBA exposes BMP, EMD (porcine amelogenins, consent), rhPDGF-BB with β-TCP

stem: Which of these is a risk factor for a less predictable regenerative outcome?
choices: A radiographic defect angle of 25° or less
ex: A thin, scalloped gingival biotype is a risk factor: with a 1-wall defect it predicted more midfacial recession after regenerative surgery (Cosyn 2012), and the 2023 risk assessment rates a thin phenotype medium (a keratinized band of 2 mm or more) or high (a narrow band or none). A thick phenotype, depth over 3 mm and a narrow angle all favor regeneration.
why: A thin, scalloped biotype predicted more midfacial recession after regenerative surgery (Cosyn 2012), and a thin phenotype rates medium to high risk in the 2023 risk assessment.
A thick phenotype is the low-risk end of the 2023 risk assessment; it's the thin, scalloped one that recedes.
Depth over 3 mm is favorable: deeper defects gained more CAL and bone, and depth had the strongest evidence.
A narrow angle (25° or less) is favorable: the defect holds the clot and graft.

likely.t: Risk factors: 1-wall anatomy, a thin scalloped biotype, smoking, plaque, the root

stem: EMD, alone or combined with graft material, produces outcomes similar to which other regenerative approach?
ex: EMD, alone or combined with graft material, produces outcomes similar to GTR. Open flap debridement is the baseline both are measured against, not an equivalent, and resection and root planing don't regenerate attachment.
why: EMD, used alone or with a graft, gives outcomes similar to GTR, the barrier-membrane approach.
Open flap debridement is the baseline (about 1.5 mm of CAL gain) that regenerative techniques are judged against, not their equal.
Osseous resection reshapes bone to eliminate the pocket; it rebuilds nothing.
Root planing heals by repair, with a long junctional epithelium, not by regeneration.

likely.t: Grafts and biologics: DFDBA exposes BMP, EMD (porcine amelogenins, consent), rhPDGF-BB with β-TCP

stem: As defined at the 1996 World Workshop, periodontal regeneration is the formation of which tissues?
choices: New bone, new cementum and new PDL
New bone and a long junctional epithelium
New cementum and new gingival epithelium
New bone and new keratinized gingiva
ex: Regeneration means new bone, new cementum and new PDL: a new functional attachment apparatus over a root that disease had exposed. Bone fill alone, or epithelium against the root, is not regeneration.
why: All three, forming a new functional attachment apparatus over a pathologically exposed root.
A long junctional epithelium against the root is repair, not regeneration.
Epithelium on the root is what regeneration tries to prevent; bone and PDL are missing too.
Keratinized gingiva is soft tissue above the attachment; cementum and PDL are missing.

likely.t: Regeneration = new bone, new cementum and new PDL, all three; a long junctional epithelium is repair

stem: What separates regeneration from repair?
choices: Regeneration restores the original architecture and function
Regeneration happens only when a membrane is placed
Repair needs a graft, while regeneration needs none
Repair forms new cementum, while regeneration doesn't
ex: Repair closes the wound without restoring the original architecture and function; regeneration rebuilds the attachment apparatus. After a flap or root planing, a root usually heals by repair: a long junctional epithelium.
why: Regeneration rebuilds bone, cementum and PDL as they were; repair heals without restoring them.
Grafts and biologics can regenerate without a membrane; GTR is one route, not the definition.
Neither term is defined by the material used: after a flap or root planing with no graft, a root usually heals by repair, and bone fill from a graft isn't regeneration on its own.
It's the reverse: new cementum is part of regeneration, while repair usually leaves epithelium on the root.

likely.t: Regeneration = new bone, new cementum and new PDL, all three; a long junctional epithelium is repair

stem: After open flap debridement, a long junctional epithelium lines the treated root. What is this healing called?
ex: Epithelium growing down the root is the usual result of flap or root-planing healing: repair. It can be stable, but it isn't a new attachment apparatus.
why: Healing without new cementum and inserting PDL fibers is repair.
Regeneration needs new cementum, PDL and bone, not epithelium against the root.
Osseointegration is bone bonding to an implant surface, not healing on a root.
Guided bone regeneration grows bone for implants on a ridge; it says nothing about the root's attachment.

likely.t: Regeneration = new bone, new cementum and new PDL, all three; a long junctional epithelium is repair

stem: Besides cells, scaffolds and growth factors, which factor in periodontal tissue regeneration does the deck list?
ex: The slide's four factors: cells, scaffolds, growth factors and blood supply.
why: Blood supply keeps the clot and the new tissue alive: the fourth factor on the slide.
Antibiotics are adjuncts for infection; they aren't one of the four factors.
Occlusal adjustment may help a mobile tooth, but it isn't one of the four factors.
Extrusion changes the bone level orthodontically; it isn't one of the four factors.

stem: Which intrabony defects gain the most CAL and bone after regenerative surgery?
choices: Deeper, narrower defects with more walls
Shallower, wider defects with more walls
Deeper, wider defects with fewer walls
Shallower, narrower defects with fewer walls
ex: "More walls, better. An angle that is more steep is better. And the depth of the defect is also important." The 2021 systematic review on the slides agrees: deeper defects with narrower angles and more walls gained more CAL and radiographic bone at 12 months.
why: Depth, a narrow angle and more walls all improve CAL and radiographic bone gain.
Shallow, wide defects gain less, even with more walls.
A wide angle and fewer walls leave nothing to contain the clot.
Shallow defects with fewer walls gain less, even with a narrow angle.

likely.t: 3-wall (most contained) defects regenerate best: more walls, a steeper angle, more depth

stem: On the slides, what does "non-supportive" defect anatomy mean?
ex: Non-supportive anatomy is a predominantly 1-wall defect, a risk factor for failure (odds ratio of 10.4 or more).
why: Non-supportive anatomy is defined as predominantly 1-wall: a risk factor for failure.
A 3-wall defect is the most supportive, the best candidate.
A circumferential defect ranks just behind the 3-wall on the decision tree, well ahead of the 1-wall.
A crater is a 2-wall defect between teeth, more supportive than a 1-wall defect.

likely.t: Risk factors: 1-wall anatomy, a thin scalloped biotype, smoking, plaque, the root

stem: Which pair of findings was a risk factor for more midfacial recession after minimally invasive regenerative surgery?
choices: A 1-wall defect and a thin, scalloped biotype
A 3-wall defect and a thick, flat biotype
A deep defect and a narrow defect angle
Heavy smoking and a long root trunk
ex: A 1-wall rather than 2-wall defect (non-supportive anatomy) and a thin, scalloped gingival biotype predicted more recession at the midfacial. Dr. Geurs said the studies behind that slide are his sources, not for you to read: know the findings.
why: Both were risk factors for more recession at the midfacial.
These are the favorable findings, not the risks.
Depth and a narrow angle favor regeneration.
Neither was a finding on the slide; root trunks were a Session 5 furcation topic.

likely.t: Risk factors: 1-wall anatomy, a thin scalloped biotype, smoking, plaque, the root

stem: Why does a 3-wall intrabony defect regenerate more predictably than a 1-wall defect?
choices: Its walls hold the clot and supply cells and vessels
Its walls stop epithelium from growing down the root
It never needs a graft, a membrane or a biologic
Its depth and width can be read exactly on a film
ex: More walls contain the defect: the clot and graft stay put, cells and vessels come from more surfaces, and the flap is held up.
why: Contained defects keep the clot and graft still and bring in cells and blood from more surfaces.
Bone walls don't block the epithelium; that is the membrane's job in GTR.
3-wall defects are still treated with grafts, membranes or biologics.
A film is 2-D; walls are confirmed at surgery, not read exactly on the radiograph.

likely.t: 3-wall (most contained) defects regenerate best: more walls, a steeper angle, more depth

stem: How is the number of remaining walls in an intrabony defect confirmed?
choices: By looking at the debrided defect at surgery
By measuring the defect angle on a periapical
By probing at six sites around the tooth
By counting the walls on a vertical bitewing
ex: A radiograph is a flat picture of a 3-D defect. The deck's opening case shows the defect from the buccal, the lingual and after debridement: that is where the walls are counted.
why: Once the flap is raised and the defect debrided, the walls can be seen directly.
The angle on a film helps select cases, but a 2-D film can't count walls reliably.
Probing finds the defect but can't show which walls remain.
Bitewings are 2-D too: walls overlap and hide each other.

likely.t: Vertical defects regenerate, horizontal bone loss doesn't; a defect obvious on a film has usually lost a wall

stem: In Laurell's 1998 meta-analysis of open flap debridement, about how much CAL was gained?
ex: Laurell 1998 (305 defects): probing depth 7.0 to 4.0 mm, CAL gain 1.5 mm, bone gain 1.1 mm. This is the baseline regeneration has to beat.
why: 1.5 mm of CAL gain, with 1.1 mm of bone gain, over 305 defects.
4 mm was the residual probing depth, not the gain.
0.2 mm is far too little; every study on the slide gained over 1 mm.
7 mm was the initial probing depth.

likely.t: Open flap debridement is the baseline (about a millimeter) every therapy must beat

stem: After open flap debridement, pockets fell from 7.0 to 4.0 mm but CAL improved only 1.5 mm. What accounts for the rest?
choices: Bone fill raising the pocket base
New cementum on the coronal root
ex: Probing depth falls by the CAL gain plus the recession. Half of the 3 mm reduction is the margin moving apically.
why: PD reduction = CAL gain + recession: 3.0 = 1.5 + 1.5.
Any rise of the pocket base is already counted in the 1.5 mm of CAL gain, and bone gain was only 1.1 mm.
New cementum would show up as CAL gain, which was only 1.5 mm.
These are averages across 305 defects, not a measuring error.

likely.t: Open flap debridement is the baseline (about a millimeter) every therapy must beat

stem: What role does open flap debridement play in the regeneration studies on the slides?
choices: The baseline that regeneration must beat
A negative control with no flap reflected
A regenerative procedure using a membrane
The test group treated with a bone graft
ex: Open flap debridement (flap, debridement, no graft) gains about 1.5 mm of CAL. Grafts, GTR and biologics are measured against it.
why: Regenerative techniques are judged by what they add to open flap debridement alone.
A flap is reflected; that's what open flap debridement means.
Debridement alone has no membrane; adding one makes it GTR.
Debridement alone has no graft; it's the comparison for graft groups.

likely.t: Open flap debridement is the baseline (about a millimeter) every therapy must beat

stem: Where does a DFDBA graft come from?
choices: The patient's own jaw or hip
A cow, processed to remove protein

stem: What does the barrier membrane do in guided tissue regeneration?

Seals the flap edges so no sutures are needed

stem: In combination therapy, what does a bone graft add under a GTR membrane?

It replaces the membrane as the epithelial barrier

It lets the membrane be removed sooner

stem: The deck follows GTR and bone-graft cases on radiographs at 1, 20 and 25 years. What did the late films show?
choices: The bone gained was still there
The bone gained had resorbed again
The defect had refilled with soft tissue
The defect had deepened past baseline

stem: Why is a non-contained intrabony defect harder to treat with a biologic such as EMD alone?
choices: Nothing holds up the flap or the clot
EMD binds only to bone walls, not root
Amelogenins are inactivated in wide defects
A flap can't be raised over the defect
ex: A non-contained defect, such as a 1-wall defect, has no walls to hold up the flap or the clot, so a biologic alone has no space to work in. These defects usually get a graft as well, to support the soft tissue, which is why the decision tree sends a 1-wall defect to combination therapy.
why: Without walls the space collapses, so these defects usually get a graft as well.

stem: Which method is the only one that can prove true periodontal regeneration?
ex: Regeneration is evaluated by histology, clinical measurements and radiographs, but only histology proves it.
why: Only a tissue section shows new cementum with inserting PDL fibers and new bone.
A probe can't tell new attachment from a long junctional epithelium.
Radiographs show bone fill, not attachment.

stem: Why can't CAL gain alone prove that regeneration happened?

CAL is measured from the moving gingival margin

Teeth aren't probed after regenerative surgery

stem: What does digital subtraction radiography show?
choices: Only the change between two standardized films
The number of walls remaining in the defect
New cementum and PDL fibers on the root

Cementum and PDL fibers need histology.

stem: What is MIST, on the deck's list of regenerative procedures?
choices: A membrane made of synthetic polymer
A mineralized bone graft from a donor
A medication that conditions the root

Membranes are GTR; MIST is a surgical technique.
Donor bone grafts are allografts such as DFDBA.
Root biomodification on the deck means EMD or PDGF, not MIST.

stem: Which two agents does the deck list under biomodification?
